Bath Library Bath Record Office Bath Royal Literary and Scientific Institution Bristol Baptist College Bristol Reference Library Devon Record Office, Exeter Dr Williams' Library, London Honiton Library John Ryland's Library, University of Manchester Public Record Office Royal National Hospital for Rheumatic Diseases Somerset Record Office, Taunton University of Bristol Library Wessex Press Library, Bath West Country Studies Library, Exeter 1The politics of civic improvement: Bath 1835-1879 with special reference to the career of Sir Jerom Murch Part 1: Subject and Rationale 1.1 The purpose and context of the research project This research project explores a municipal response to improvement politics, from the election of the first reformed council of 1835 to the emergence of social citizenship in the late 1870s: a philosophy which recognised civic duty as a spiritual function and agent of moral improvement (1). The changing nature of civic consciousness will be identified both in relation to the new perception of the council as an agent of improvement and the interplay of individual versus corporate initiative in the achievement of material progress. The political, social and intellectual elites will be considered through an analysis of committee activists to ascertain networks of influence and assess the scope of municipal power. As such the project seeks to make a contribution to the understanding of urban history. Particularly from the late sixteenth century and the influences of the Renaissance, specific interests in researching the histories of individual towns have exercised local antiquarians and propagandists (2). This movement was revitalised in the mid-nineteenth century by a development of historical research techniques and renewed interest in the past (3), particularly the medieval period which provided a model for the Ecclesiological movement in architecture and also a focus for localist agitation against government growth. Structured, analytical work on the changing role, composition and associated configurations of power within municipal councils was only addressed from the late 1950s e.g. A. Birch's study 2of Glossop (4); R. Dahl's work concerning New Haven (5) and G. Jones's consideration of Wolverhampton (6). This field of research became a part of the new discipline of urban history, pioneered as a discrete subject area by the late Prof. H. Dyos in the 1960s, a time when urbanisation, suburbanisation and conurbation had been developed phenomena for over half a century with urban areas housing a steady 80% of the population, the saturation point for population within urban developments (7). Nineteenth century interest in cities and their attendant social problems was developed by the publication of the Utilitarian inspired statistical surveys of the 1830s and 1840s. Manchester in particular became the "shock city" and model for the new interest in social theorising (8). The resultant campaigns against filth and fever concentrated the minds of reformers and they devised improvement measures to confront these first manifestations of industrial urban crisis. They also faced the associated political implications concerning the duties of central and local governments, the extent of personal freedoms and the viability of the "self-help" society (9). It was essentially an urban middle-class crisis, as this sector of society formed the majority of the urban elite and championed individualistic achievement to justify its challenge to upper-class hegemony. The urban arena was theirs as the county arena was dominated by the upper classes. In 1959 Asa Briggs termed 1783-1867 "The Age of Improvement" (10), as he saw the period as characterised by an optimistic faith in reform and the intrinsic value of progress. Religious revivalism with its attendant humanitarian impulse, coupled with the heightened political awareness of civil rights which stemmed from the revolutionary experiences of the eighteenth century, provided the background for the improvements. The Evangelical component in improvement politics created the distinctive moral dimension which was lacking in the earlier 3concepts of improvement as formulated by urban groups of Improvement Commissioners created by private Acts of Parliament. The period was dominated by the legislative triumphs of the middle class, notably the 1832 Reform Act and the repeal of the Corn Laws in 1846, and the attempts of the affluent to obtain social control and avoid insurrection during a period of demographic and philosophical turmoil. In 1848, the year of the first national Public Health Act, Marx and Engels responded to this and denounced, "philanthropists, humanitarians, improvers ..., organisers ..., temperance fanatics, hole-and-corner reformers of every imaginable kind," (11) but the period addressed in this project saw little progress for party based socialism as a political force after the collapse of Owenite utopianism. The initiative in improvement politics was taken briefly by the Utilitarian theorists in the 1830s, alienating Tory and working-class opponents of centralised bureaucracy. Tory humanitarian paternalism eclipsed Radical endeavours by the late 1840s and fused with incipient impulses to municipal socialism to create a multi-party groundswell of liberal enthusiasm for civic action in the urban environment. Briggs identified the end of "The Age of Improvement" with the passing of the 1867 Reform Act. Certainly, Bagehot's conceptions of parliamentary life were outdated by this extension of the franchise and a workers' class consciousness began to emerge, but progress was slow and the Liberal middle-class ethic was not challenged until the 1880s. Before this, middle-class attempts to exert social control can be discerned in the raising of municipal consciousness through the activities of middle-class urban elites. In municipal terms, the later 1870s were important for improvement politics. The years of Chamberlain's mayoralties in Birmingham, 1873-76, made the civic gospel theories of Dawson a reality of "gas and water socialism", the inaccurate 4and popular description of Chamberlain's policy which originated in extreme socialist criticism of Fabian support for municipal trading (12). The policy has perhaps been more realistically labelled, "municipal capitalism", by D. Fraser (13) whose work, like that of Briggs (14), has recognised the application of individualism within a municipal context. In the extreme case of the emergence of a coherent civic gospel entrepreneurial endeavours were made by the corporation as a religious duty on behalf of the community. It was ironic that popular belief in individualism included support for local self-government yet the development of municipal responsibilities and collectivism on a local level facilitated the emergence of centralisation with a socialist base. The new concept of civic consciousness was disseminated during the final stages of the Gladstonian Liberal consensus before the discord of 1886 and the growth of the new Socialism through the work of individuals like Hyndman, Morris and Sidney Webb. Mellor's work on the, "Civic Renaissance", of Bristol between 1865-75 (15) underlined the significance of the period for the municipalities. Civic authorities were motivated by the desire to create social citizenship and establish the city as an inspirational force and focus of loyalty through environmental and cultural improvements in the middle class Liberal tradition. The urban historians of the 1960s approached their subject with an enthusiastic, modernist optimism reminiscent of the social engineering of the 1860s and 1870s. Primary Victorian improvements had been overlaid by post-war solutions, with shopping centres and high rise accommodation characterising the new approach to tackling the creeping obsolescence of the nineteenth century response and the damage caused by war. The planners of the 1960s appeared unaware that they might be creating another set of urban problems for the late twentieth century. Dyos coordinated the seminal conference of the Urban History Group in 1966 at the University of Leicester which brought together researchers with historical, 5political, sociological, geographical and civic design skills to create a synthesis of views and provide a broad platform for the future consideration of urban history. Apart from detailed methodological discussions, a major issue discussed at the conference was the necessity for comparative studies of British cities in order to 

provide more empirical material from which to formulate generalisations concerning the nineteenth century urban experience. The conference provided an opportunity for E. Hennock to develop his 1956 PhD 

thesis, concerning the municipal government of Birmingham 1865-76, to a consideration of municipal attitudes to reform and analyses of council composition in both Birmingham and Leeds. Seven years later an extended version of this paper was published as the definitive study of the nature of the councils in these cities and contemporary notions of the role of a municipal council (16). This study of civic concerns in industrial cities developed the lines of enquiry initiated by Asa Briggs in 1963 with the publication of his work, "Victorian cities" (17) which included Birmingham and Leeds amongst the chosen six examples. Briggs's work itself was in the spirit of Kitson Clark's earlier publication, "The making of Victorian England" in which he considered the "high noon" of Victorian achievement between 1850-1875 and emphasised the need for a study of local institutions and the individuals within them as a contribution to the dialogue on municipal initiative in the age of reform. As he observed, the study of the most individual of individuals adds to our knowledge of society as a whole (18), providing a counter-balance to the statisticians penchant to rely on, 

"bloodless units of generalisation" (19) and the tendency of the indignant school of historians to offer partizan inspired caricatures without recourse to specific examples. A more recent example of work concentrating on one town and an individual within it is M. Harrison's thesis on social reform in Manchester which specifically referred to the work of T. C. Horsfall, a local activist (20). 6Briggs stressed the need for the effects of the reforms of 1835 to be fully examined and advocated that historians should be, "peering as through a microscope at the local forces in politics - individuals, clubs, parties and pressure groups" (21), rather than accepting generalised national trends and seeking to make the subject town fit the pattern. He advocated that the unique experiences of individual towns of all types should be studied, as older towns exhibiting Victorian elements in their development were as relevant as those industrial centres which had grown rapidly and developed distinctive socio-economic characters in the nineteenth century itself. In his view it was in the study of the interplay of local interests that the strength of provincialism as a social force may be assessed (22). This point was echoed in the 1966 Leicester Conference. R. Newton's paper on relations between society and political leadership in nineteenth century Exeter, a decaying town with an obsolete society, was viewed as an important contrast with work on the expanding towns, allowing a fuller appreciation of national developments to be gained (23). Generalisations concerning "Victorian" cities need to be checked and balanced by findings from research done on the older boroughs to see how they responded to, or neglected, the challenges of the permissive government legislation of the nineteenth century. Interesting research has been done to provide a model for the analysis of municipal power. J. Garrard's work, Leaders and politics in nineteenth century Salford (24) led to his publication in 1983 which provided a comparative consideration of community power 1830-1880 in Rochdale, Bolton and Salford (25). This work embraced his earlier suggestions for a framework for community power analysis (26) and advanced beyond a consideration of 7recruitment, such as that undertaken by Hennock, to an appreciation of the dynamics within the urban political arena. In his view the configurations of power operating within a town were more complex than a simple elitist model as advanced by earlier studies e.g. those of Birch and Jones. Garrard also criticised Dahl, who in his view only offered a structured analysis of the contemporary scene, and lapsed into an unquestioning acceptance of the unfettered autonomy of council action when dealing with the nineteenth century. Garrard did not suggest that a pluralist situation allowing full bargaining between all interested parties existed in nineteenth century towns, but contended that sufficient constraints on action existed to render an elitist, "urban squire-archy", interpretation unsound. He believed that the socio-economic elite of a town may have appeared to hold the majority of political resources, i.e. all varieties of influence, but their activities were severally constrained by a number of forces which complicated direct or effective action and which could often condemn the apparently patrician and powerful council to the wilderness of, "non-decisional politics" (27). Pressure may have been exerted on councils both by groups within the elite who were excluded from office and from the lower echelons of society within the town. In the case of Bath, Graham Davis's research has revealed that the social elite of the town were forced to contest for power outside the political arena, which was dominated by the commercial ruling class, and occasionally act in concert with the working class in order to influence the council (28). Similarly, the continued existence of earlier authority groups like Improvement Commissioners could complicate direct action by the council, as could the paid council official and expert who became increasingly important towards the close of the century e.g. A. Alexander observed that in 1873 a part-time town clerk 8was sought in preference to a full-time appointment as the latter might obtain too much influence and inhibit the activity of the councillors (29). Outside the council chamber, vested interests within the town and its hinterland were also important influences on council effectiveness and were not necessarily controlled by the councillors. Such controls as isolated by Garrard need to be considered in any analysis of the effectiveness of a council. D. Fraser has demonstrated that the central conflict for supremacy in municipal politics was that between rival sectors of the town elite and he proposed a model for comprehending the municipal political experience (30). He saw the political life experienced by a town dweller to be politicised at four different levels; at vestry meetings, council elections, parliamentary elections and amongst the unofficial forces of political agitation. This view conflicts with Marxist interpretations such as that offered by J. Foster who based his analysis of political action in a town on the level of class consciousness and conflict generated within its society (31). In line with Fraser's work, the emphasis of research has moved from the working class experience to consider that of the middle class (32). However, most work has been done on industrial cities and therefore the findings will not necessarily provide a fit with the experience of an older town such as Bath. This work does not seek to use the Bath experience to test specific political models, but by incorporating useful observations made by earlier theorists it seeks to shed light on evolving perceptions of the role of local government. Critical narrative has revived as a popular scholarly form of the communication of research findings, as quantification methods and rigidly determinist approaches have been discredited e.g. L. Stone wrote of the subject in 1979 (33) as did Angus Buchanan in 1991 (34). Partizan political historians, cliometricians and ecological demographers sought simplistic causation and failed. Interest in, "how 9many" has been superseded by interest in changing definitions of terms and conceptions of reality, with the extreme post-modernists and post-structuralists favouring the "linguistic turn" and challenging the existence of any reality outside our linguistic articulations (35). Accepting that complete historical truth is unobtainable, it is in the tradition of an examination of "mentalite" (36) that this work lies, in seeking to ascertain the varied contemporary perceptions of the role of the council. Reformed nineteeth century town councils appear superficially similar to their twentieth century counterparts, with familiar elected representatives on fixed terms of office, but they were formed for a far more restricted purpose. Perceptions of their role had enlarged significantly by the late 1870s but throughout the century councils varied widely one from another and varied within each municipality over time. Also, as Garrard has demonstrated, scholarly assumptions concerning the easy sway of power exercised by councils composed of members of the local elite have been over simplistic, council action being inhibited by a variety of forces which complicate an assessment of their intentions. However, there was some consensus concerning the nature and role of a councillor in 1835. The essential requirements were popularly accepted to be station and respectability. Substantial property owners and rate payers were presumed to be the most likely burgesses to be intelligent, educated and have interests co-terminus with those of the borough. The main intention of the Municipal Reform Act had been to allow wealthy, intelligent, educated Dissenters to assist the Anglican elite in protecting and administering the properties and incomes of the borough. The only obligatory duty of the reformed councils was to form a police force, which emphasised the role of the council as the keeper of the peace, dispenser of justice and protector of property. Early developments of the role of the council occurred when individual councils extended the scope of 10 local improvements acts. For example, the Police Commissioners in Manchester ran a municipal gas works as early as 1817. Similarly, in 1846 Liverpool devised and obtained a Sanitary Act which provided a model for future national public health legislation and also installed the first borough Medical Officer of Health. The following year the council purchased the interests of two local water companies. However, such action was not driven by a cogent philosophy concerning the role of the council but was in response to urgent, individual needs. Revolutionary conceptions of the role of a municipal council can be dated from the early 1860s and the promulgation of Birmingham's civic gospel. This was instigated by the preaching of George Dawson, a charismatic figure whose oratorical skills captivated a range of orthodox and heterodox Dissenters after he accepted the ministry at the Baptist Chapel of Mount Zion, Graham St. Birmingham in 1844. As Hennock demonstrated, Dawson initiated the new municipal philosophy and expounded it in the early 1860s in the Church of the Saviour, constructed for him in 1847 in the style of a lecture theatre rather than a church (37). He believed that the town was the local manifestation of the nation with corresponding duties to its inhabitants. The town was likened to a family, a

distinct organism and a new church, providing a unified, godly community. In response to the continual sectarian controversies which hindered development in 

towns, an elevated form of municipal unity was to be acknowledged which rose above creedal divisions. There was a distinctly nationalistic flavour in such a theory and Hennock discovered the source of this to be Dawson's espousal of the causes of continental nationalism given a, "local twist" (38). Dawson believed that municipal government was, "a solemn organism through which shall flow and in which shall be shaped all the highest, loftiest and truest ends of man's intellectual and moral nature" (39). Religious life was to be lived through social 1 1 and political duty. The corporation was to be the primary agent of social improvement acknowledging its duties and recognising, as Chamberlain did, that there was no nobler sphere of activity save imperial politics (40). In its most extreme form as expemplified in Birmingham it was an all embracing civic strategy. John T. Bunce, editor of the Birmingham Daily Post and an associate of Chamberlain's during this period, wrote that the true municipality should, "completely grasp the life of the community ... expressing the communal idea" (41). Briggs has seen in Dawson's theme an heroic appeal reminiscent of the writing of Carlyle (42). Although not a supporter of the nineteenth century church, Carlyle's message of a spiritual approach to life to counter the excessive materialism of the age could have been inspirational, as could his belief in the interconnection of all life's themes. The liberal scholar T. H. Green provided a philosophical basis for the development of collectivist theory which fused the desire for reform with the religiosity of the period (43). He denounced Utilitarianism and insensitive Spencerian individualism, to follow his assumptions developed from Hegel's theories which stressed the organic nature of society, the individual depending on the community to secure a full and satisfactory life whilst having a responsibility for social reform which would lead to moral improvement. However, he rejected the Hegelian emphasis on a development of centralization to the detriment of local initiative. He brought a religious sanction to citizenship through his work in the mid-Victorian period, equating spiritual with civic functions and practicing what he preached as a member of Oxford town council (44). Apart from the philosophical influences, the widening of the franchise which increased demand for social reform, the increasing tendency for workmen and employers to combine and the foreign challenges to British trading supremacy were conducive to the development of Dawson's ideas. Collectivism 12 and the desire to protect the interests of society as a whole superseded the appeal of individualism. Central to the emergence of the civic gospel of Birmingham was the desire to elevate the municipal body in the cause of spreading education to the inhabitants. The Dissenting personnel (particularly the powerful Unitarian lobby) within the National Education League, who sought universal, unsectarian education approved of the civic gospel theory. Provision of education to the bulk of the population had been an ancient duty of the church and was dominated by the National School establishments of the Church of England. The civic gospel elevated the council to the status of a religious force and imbued it with ecclesiastical dignity. Although the council was not synonymous with the School Boards which were eventually elected after the passing of the 1870 Education Act, the impetus behind Dawson's message and the philosophy of Chamberlain, co-founder of the National Education League, who monopolised the council as Mayor over the years 1873-6 and packed it with members of the socio-economic elite, was a desire to educate and improve. The new, high calibre councillors saw their work as a privilege and part of their religious obligation. R. W. Dale the Congregationalist disciple of Dawson enlarged the message of the civic gospel to appeal to the evangelical wing of Protestant dissent that baulked at the overtly secular appeal of Dawson. Dale's understanding encompassed the civic gospel as a rediscovered function of the church, not an escape from Evangelicalism. Joseph Chamberlain made the civic gospel a reality and inspired other municipalities to experiment with municipal socialism. In common with members of the other leading Unitarian families in Birmingham, the Nettlefold's (his relatives and business partners), the Kenricics (the family of his first two wives) and the Martineaus, Chamberlain was an early devotee of Dawson's civic 13 gospel. Entering the council in 1869 he worked to elevate the reputation of the municipal body and the importance of social issues with the council taking responsibility for both the quality of life enjoyed by the people and the future of the city. Enriched by ecclesiastical terminology, the accepted job description of a councillor became a fit calling for members of the urban elite. In Chamberlain's view the church was relegated to the position of a less effective proto-type of the corporation (45). During the peak phase of the municipal take-overs of gas concerns between 1869-1878, Birmingham Town Council purchased the local gas works in 1875. Chamberlain capitalised on the economic advantages of this to finance other schemes such as the purchase of the water companies in 1876 and the slum clearance and redevelopment programme. Birmingham was run as an efficient business. In Chamberla'in's words, "The town will be parked, paved, assized, marketed, Gas and Watered and improved - all as the result of three years active work" (46). Manchester's early administrative improvements and mid-century dominance stemming from the reputation of the Manchester School of Politics, Cobden, Bright, Free Trade and internationalism were overshadowed by Birmingham. Chamberlain's Birmingham offered a collectivist, nationalistic, protectionist message, more in tune with the tenor of the last quarter of the century and the philosophy of the civic gospel was an important part of this message. The theory and practice of Birmingham revolutionised the way in which councils were perceived and created an ideal of council behaviour which pertained until the late nineteenth century when the role of central government eclipsed that of the locality. By examining other towns in the light of Birmingham's civic gospel a wider perspective can be given to the phenomenon. However, it is important 14 not to confuse civic pride or a partial acceptance of a noble or quasi-religious role for the council with the totality of vision achieved in Birmingham. A civic gospel was a rare manifestation. As Briggs pointed out, even Sheffield with a mobile society and network of small independent businesses similar to those in Birmingham did not have a civic gospel (47). Birmingham was a pioneer in this respect, requiring a particularly thorough movement to provide an impetus to improvement after years of council activity which had been characterised by short sighted economy and incompetence. The council had been derisively christened, "The Woodman regime", after the public house in which the council meetings often took place (48). Birmingham also had the energetic input of outsiders such as Dawson, Dale and Chamberlain to spearhead the movement and revitalise local thought. If contributions of such individuals are to be assessed realistically, then other individuals in other towns need to be investigated. M. Thompson refuted attempts to identify benefactors as promulgators of the civic gospel and observed that Chamberlain as paradigm of civic gospel leader of the urban elite is in danger of being the sole example of his kind (49). A civic gospel leader would have social influence in the key urban networks but unlike many philanthropists would also be imbued with a sense of sacred mission as well as civic responsibility. The notion of the civic gospel is useful out of its Birmingham context as it highlights three imperatives of the nineteenth century provincial psyche; the intensely localised purview, burgeoning municipal pride accelerated by the proliferation of new borough charters and lastly, excessive religiosity. These features coalesced in the civic gospel theory where the mission of the corporation transcended its personnel and the socio-economic divisions within the city. Socialist collectivism, itself a secular aim, was expressed in religious terms by latter-day Owenites such as William Morris and George Bernard Shaw in their 15 individual approaches to the new faith where the new God was political truth and the devil, capitalism. J. Redmond has explored the significance of the religious dimension, showing that although Morris favoured the inclinations of the individual and Shaw the importance of the state above individual needs, both conceptualised politics in religious terms (50). The civic gospel theory of the traditionally religious urban middle-class provides an example of the contemporary interface between religion and politics. The role of the Nonconformists is particularly crucial, as their faith remained essentially a political statement, though positions were less polarised than in the mid 1830s which marked the height of antagonism between Church and Dissent. Hegel's concept of the Volksgeist had emphasised the importance of a non-Christian folk religion following Rousseau's support for a 'religion civile' and this provided a philosophical platform for the future development of municipal mission, which in the case of Birmingham provided a civic gospel. Research by Cannadine and also by Trainor (51) has discussed the concept of a civic religion as a safe transference of the desire for pomp and ceremony, ritual and worship, from the battleground of Protestant sectarianism to the unifying fold of the municipal faith, presided over by the dramatically robed figure of His Worship, the local mayor. Garrard has drawn attention to the crucial importance of the personality of the mayor in the nineteenth century municipalities, observing that the mayor had scope to function as the initiator and director of council policy (52). The municipal reform of 1835 developed the role of mayor: a Bath commentator remarked on the enlarged role of the mayor, his extended duties and significantly greater legal and moral powers (53). With the mayor at the head, a devotional hierarchy was constructed, revering the concept of the city and embodying its pride to provide a focus for consensual partizanship and public theatre to pull together the diverse strands of the urban world. Such a 16 transference released isolated, polarised groups and made social development possible but did not necessarily involve a sense of unified mission. It would be fallacious to describe such features of "civic religion" as a civic gospel, although it does incorporate facets of it. Studies of nineteenth century municipal government after 1835 are of particular importance because of the localised nature of social and political life. At the start of the period governmental activity was primarily at the local level as central government concentrated on national policy matters and interference in the daily running of town life was not deemed to be its concern. Before the 1880s government activity had grown substantially but notions of centralisation and collectivism were persistently unpopular. Bagehot found the English dislike of executive government a, "curious peculiarity", which did not manifest itself in the attitudes of the Americans, French or Swiss where the executive was believed to have the mandate of the people. Traditionally hostile to despotic central government, the English provinces viewed state interference as tyrannical, "alien action", even in 1867 (54). Similarly Bagehot's fellow Liberal, J. S. Mill, commented on the, "unreasoning prejudice", of English localists against even the most benevolent of centrally inspired innovations (55). These attitudes bolstered the new found faith in corporations, newly cleansed and rendered politically acceptable by the reform of 1835. The localist movement of the 1850s led by writers such as J. Toulmin Smith stressed the connection between loyalty and locality, and encouraged suspicion of the centre and the revival of enthusiasm for the idealised past of Saxon independence and local self-government centring on the parish (56). Ironically, this movement, triggered by the dissatisfaction felt for life in an industrial society of large scale economies, revivified the Parliamentary defence of its own antiquity in the seventeenth century. The theory of the tradition of an ancient constitution originating in the Witenagemot 17 and reaching through the Curia Regia to Simon de Montfort's parliament was utilised on behalf of the local organs of government to restrict the development of the centre. Over the period considered by this project, Benthamism, the doctrines of political economy and self help gave way to state action and the growth of collectivism on a national scale. Scholarly debate from the late 1950s to the mid-1970s challenged Dicey's original thesis (57) of a 1865 threshold for the change from one controlling philosophy to the other and reconsidered the nature of the administrative revolution and its timing. MacDonagh's reappraisal of 1958 was the seminal work, suggesting a pre-1865 theory of self-generating administrative reform following initial legislation to combat intolerable social evils (58). Similarly, Roberts identified the foundation of sixteen central agencies between 1833-48 and saw in this growth the origins of the welfare state (59). Benthamism, dismissed by MacDonagh as merely a part of the zeitgeist of early nineteenth century life and not a causal factor in administrative revolution has been reappraised as a synthesis of individualist and collectivist impulses. Hart (60), supported by Midwinter, identified the Benthamite "preventive ideal" in operation before the late 1860s and although acknowledging collectivist impulses stemming from this philosophy they were viewed as ineffectual, with local agencies conducting only perfunctory communications with the centre (61). Academic debate continued with Lubenow's construction of a dichotomy of conflicting governmental roles: the traditional role resting on historic rights and customs versus the incrementalist role which countenanced empirical change in response to need without a formal commitment to collectivist theory (62). Fraser's synthesis admitted a partial recognition of this in describing administrative revolution through ad hoc responses of state to social problems (63). 18 The English retained their partiality for local autonomy and suspected any form of centralisation. In the civic sphere sectors of local elites competed for power and influence. As Garrard observed, within the towns the local political arena was not only important but also highly visible and fascinating to the inhabitants (64). Local politicians were well known to the people of all classes and a degree of communal satisfaction was gained by observing the rituals of civic dignitaries and reading about their social and philanthropic endeavours in the local newspapers. Despite the railways, the orbit of the town was the limit of the social and economic vision for the majority at least to the end of the 1880s. Although he warned against the, "selfish mismanagement", of some local oligarchies (65) J. S. Mill praised the borough in his 1861 treatise on "Representative Government" (66) as the ideal initiator of legislation, given that improvement legislation was the businesss of the locality and its ratepayers. Local initiative had to isolate a need, plan how to finance it and obtain the right to do so by obtaining an appropriate Act of Parliament. Local acts proliferated even after general improvement legislation began with the Poor Law Amendment Act of 1834. The numerous Clauses Acts of 1845 and 1847, which simplified drafting and related to railways, land, town improvements, markets and fairs, encouraged local initiative still further (67). Mill recognised the local councils as educational opportunities for the lesser minds in the community to mix with the greater and subsequently elevate themselves (68). Ideally, information would emanate from the centre, enabling locally financed institutions to resolve problems. Therefore, the councillors were the initiators of legislation, the representative body for the municipality and also the executive arm. They could appoint officials who were totally subordinated to the council until the increasing 19 complexity of business and rise of professionalism in their employees made such control impossible. From 1835 until the 1880s local councillors not only dictated policy but also attended to the minutiae of administration. The influence of central government was minimal and legislation was largely discretionary. The unpopularity of the first effort at centralised control, the Poor Law Board, inhibited the early development of further control and government influence was limited to negative measures such as the withholding of grants or the publication of incriminating statistics concerning conditions within the towns. It was only in the 1890s that the characteristic independence of local government bodies was partially eclipsed by Whitehall. Garrard viewed the decay of the locality as a prime feature in the changing social and political life of the people. The increasing dominance of Whitehall, the movement of the middle class out of the cities to the counties or suburban developments and increased mobility of the work force caused a decline in the power of the locality to dominate the interests of the individual. In his opinion, local social leaders ceased to exist (69). Therefore, the period considered in this research project is the brief heyday of municipal self determination (70), administered by councils elected by an increasingly democratic franchise. It has been traditionally suggested that the development of an honest, competent system of local government was achieved in the nineteenth century and that this was a distinguishing and original feature of the period, enabling the provision of a civilised social life (71). Such praise is merited by the aim of the Victorian effort if not by the final effect, certainly as achieved by 1870, Woodward's closing date. Only relative honesty, competence and civilisation were achieved with the squalid findings of Rowntree in 1901 and Booth 1889-1907 placing the nineteenth century achievement in perspective. The municipalities, without 20 effective supervision until after the "high noon" of Victorianism, were relatively free to neglect their inhabitants or to provide individual solutions for their problems within the scope of the discretionary acts. Their activities illustrate the early struggles between individualism and collectivism which still dominate political life. The nineteenth century municipal experience in Bath has been neglected until recently, eclipsed by the sanitised Roman/Georgian legacy fostered by the nineteenth century civic elite as part of the campaign to attract not only new residents, but also the elusive visitors whom they still believed were the key to the further development of the local economy. Phillips observed in 1973 (72) that surprisingly little interest had been shown in Bath by professional historians, apart from R. S. Neale's contributions of the 1960s and 1970s. Neale's researches were limited to the first half of the century and offered a study of Bath in accordance with his model of class orientation which developed the standard three class Marxist interpretation to five. The Philosophic Radicals of the "middling-class" were recognised as the dynamic element in politics, but the balance of power within the civic elite and its relation to the social elite were not considered (73). Similarly, a more recent thesis covering the 1837-1848 period has contributed to the debate on politics in Bath offering another interpretation of working-class movements and challenging Neale's assumptions concerning Whig/Radical and Chartist/Radical relations. McNulty's work stressed that Radicalism was not totally extinguished in Bath after 1847 but does not acknowledge that Tory dominance gained at this time was purely temporary (74). Phillips' work on religion in Bath during the nineteenth century examined its role and related it to secular developments. It was concluded that Bath was a

stagnant, dejected community at all levels from labourer to gentleman; religious 21 yet lacking the zest for sectarian conflict and exhibiting a lack lustre, spiritless tolerance. This is at odds with the fiercely partizan nature of Bath in the 1830s and 1840s and the article ignored the partial revivification of the fortunes of the town as a resort in the 1870s which continued beyond the end of the century. Similarly, Jeremy's article on the decline of Bath as social centre and Kite's dissertation on library facilities have emphasised decay (75), and Hope and later Simpson's studies of educational provision have over-emphasised the dominance of right wing conservatism (76). A thesis by Wadsworth (77) has considered the purely recreational aspects of nineteenth century Bath, an architectural appraisal was completed in 1991 (78) and individuals have published short articles on isolated features of the period (79). The most recent research on nineteenth century Bath to address the urban experience in the wider sense has been done by Graham Davis (80) who developed Dyos's urban history concept of image and reality and used a working class area of Bath as an example of the working class experience in a provincial city. The work utilised research findings to confront a perceived reality with a reconstruction of structural reality and thereby extend understanding of the Victorian experience. In the conclusion of the work, it was suggested that the systematic study of the networks of influence in Bath and the nature of municipal power still needed to be identified to improve understanding of Bath society. The concept of social citizenship characterised the mid and late Victorian middle-class response to the challenge of urban living. In the newly developed towns the municipalisation of cultural institutions was a common manifestation of this as the council sought to forge a common culture and capture the imaginations of the inhabitants (81). Bath was different, it was a pre-industrial city with a clear self-image based on the business created by visitors to the springs. The influence of Ruskin's inspirational work, "The Stones of Venice" completed by 1853 was not 22 required to bring Italian style celebrating municipal glory and the identification of citizen with city, as a unique manifestation of the eighteenth century landscape movement in towns had developed Bath to the closest approximation of Palladio's vision in the country. These facts acted as a retardant to effective action. By 1879 Bath still had no free art gallery or library, and though the former shortcoming was rectified by the close of the century it was 1924 before a free lending library was provided (82). However, the council had secured all the legislative acts it required by the close of the 1870s to confirm its supremacy as principal organ of social improvement. As has already been shown by Graham Davis, the rhetoric of one individual raised Bath Council above the usual petty level of business to a nobler vision of nineteenth century municipal endeavour (83). The most prominent civic dignitary of Bath in the post-1835 era was Sir Jerom Murch, a Unitarian Liberal and ex-pastor with influence in the socio-economic, intellectual and political elites of the city and viewed as the civic consensus politician par excellence; the "type (archetypal) Mayor" (84), or "Model Mayor" (85) an office he held on seven occasions between 1863 and 1892, which was a record equalled only by William Sherston, mayor in the late sixteenth and early seventeenth centuries. Mayoral lists reveal that Murch's nearest rival in Bath since the reform of local government was William Hunt the Radical who was chief magistrate on five occasions. Murch was at different times a councillor, alderman and mayor; president of Liberal associations and clubs; stalwart of education committees and school governing bodies, the Poor Law Board, social, literary and scientific institutions. He was a philanthropist, fund raiser, author and eventually a Deputy Lieutenant of the county. As the Bath Year Book of 1896 observed, "almost every local institution which could claim to exist for the public good had to place on record its grateful recognition of services which he had rendered". Murch's obituary in 23 the Bath Herald (86) observed that his life was representative of local history over the previous half century. Although no charismatic leader of men, Murch's influence over the council was, according to the Bath Journal (87) "only at rare intervals resisted". He is a useful focus of research as he operated within the High Church, Low Church, Nonconformist, literary and fashionable elites, intermeshing the civic and unofficial networks of influence in the city. This individual provides a case study through which to explore responses to the politics of improvement on a personal level as, more than any other individual, he appears to have been instrumental in raising civic consciousness within the City of Bath. 24 References Part 1: Subject and Rationale 1.1 The purpose and context of the research project 1. Bath Journal 18th May, 1895. 30 1.2 The City of Bath and its status pre 1835 Before consideration is given to Murch's position in Bath society and the nature of the city's improvement politics, it is necessary to consider the background to civic activity and responsibility and the type of community which developed in the city. Urban settlement originated on the site because of the natural facilities of the hot springs and convenient crossings over the River Avon. A Roman town, Aquae Sulis, was built to utilise the springs and the Saxon settlement which succeeded it was important enough to have its own mint, in common with ten other towns in the region (1). Bath featured in the Gesta Stephani of 1138 which indicated that the hot springs were of national repute and attractive to visitors both sick and healthy (2). The city had become a monastic and cloth producing centre with a Merchant Guild of sufficient stature to receive the city's first Royal Charter in 1189 (3). By 1590 an Elizabethan charter vested full powers of municipal government in the corporation. However, the dissolution of the monasteries and the decay of the cloth trade in the south-west had reduced Bath's prosperity. B. Cunliffe has suggested that the third quarter of the sixteenth century marked the decline of Bath's dependence on wool and the emergence of the city as a tourist centre as the corporation established control over the property previously owned by the Priory, including the rights to the springs (4). However, a publication of 1673 suggested that the new economic strategy of Bath as a resort town was only then beginning to emerge. It stated that the waters had been, "scarce ever made known (at leastwise made use of) till ... within this two or three years". The author, Henry Chapman, sometime mayor and councillor who was committed to the re-launch of the city as a resort, energetically countered the lack of national publicity for 31 the waters and recommended Bath to Charles II and fashionable society as an, "ancient, famous, little pretty city" (5). S. McIntyre's research into the rise of Bath between the late seventeenth and early nineteenth centuries to, "pleasure capital of Georgian England" (6), has shown that the city was the first in the country to make the transformation from a predominantly manufacturing economy to one dominated by the needs of spa visitors. The development of specialised spa resorts has been suggested to be part of a wider renaissance of provincial culture which took place between 1680 and 1760 as a response to the Post-Restoration enthusiasm for leisure and luxury (7). This concept has been challenged by A. McInnes, largely on semantic issues, but the growth of urban specialisation in response to the leisure imperative has been acknowledged (8). This development of urban culture provides an interesting parallel with the nineteenth century development of municipal consciousness which is the theme of this research project on Bath. However, Bath's nineteenth century experience was not to provide the archetypal example of a component of revival as it did in the eighteenth century "renaissance". As the city experienced its major population expansion in the eighteenth century, Bath provides an example of the evolution of the civic role without the sharp spurs to progress experienced by expanding, industrialising cities such as Manchester and Birmingham. Bath's unreformed council played a central role in the development of Bath during the last forty years of the eighteenth century when the appearance of the city was transformed into the most sustained example of late-Renaissance classicism in the country. McIntyre aimed to place novel emphasis on the role of the council and explained its entry into development during the late 1760s as a

result of the increased confidence, wealth and vision of the members which were 32 gained as the town expanded (9). Her research found the councillors to be active and effective, even in comparison with many nineteenth century counterparts, as they succeeded in speculative building projects and before these, in acquiring pioneering Acts of Parliament (10) e.g. 1707 Turnpike and Improvement Act (6 Anne c 42) which included clauses for paving, lighting and cleansing to codify existing practises. However, in Neale's researches the council did not emerge as innovatory, being neither the originator or unanimous supporter of an important City Act of 1766 (6 Geo III c.70) which facilitated the start of the remodelling of the centre and replaced parochial improvement officials with a body of City Commissioners, although he did recognise substantial civic involvement (11). Neale calculated the average figure' of municipal indebtedness to have increased from £2,764 in the 

early 1760s to £54,020 in the 1790s as the council abandoned paternalistic, social and economic corporatism and chose to behave as any other aggressive, individualistic developer (12). Self interest and glorification were identified as motivating factors but, as they were a civic group not acting as individuals or private owners, a more generous interpretation might view the council's action as a manifestation of civic pride and entrepreneurial capitalisation. Cunliffe estimated the population to be approximately 2,000 in 1700 (13), which had increased to 33,196 by 1801 (14) as a response to the demands of the visitors for medical and social facilities. These figures do not reveal the effects of the visitors themselves, for as an anonymous writer of 1700 observed, the city was as populous as London for the five month season (15). Therefore, council neglect of the potential opportunities might have been construed as a squandering of talents. The council interpreted its role as developer of the wealth and property of the city 33 and provider of facilities for the visitors. Coincidentally, this involvement developed a responsibility for water supply which was piped before the end of the sixteenth century and was of benefit to the populace as a whole. Later in the nineteenth century a municipal supply of water became a fundamental tenet of urban improvement politics and Bath ensured that civic powers were not allowed to lapse as they had in other boroughs such as Norwich (16). Bath's 1766 Improvement Act (6 Geo III c.70) provided for powers of entry on private land within two miles of the city, except that belonging to the Duke of Kingston which constituted approximately one-fifth of the old town (17), and the right to break up a highway or common for the provision and maintenance of an adequate water supply (18). City Commissioners became involved with the removal of nuisances to improve conditions such as those cited in Wood's book of 1765 which claimed that all the principal ways in the town, common to man and beast, had offensive gutters and were as inconvenient as possible (19). In 1842, Chadwick's report on the sanitary condition of the labouring population showed initial approval for Bath Council's supply, which catered for 75% of the acknowledged needs of the city and included five free public pumps. Four other agencies organised by private landlords delivered supplies to parts of the city, but Chadwick still identified Bath as a model for corporation water supply (20) which could solve the problems of wasteful private competition. As well as wide powers of water supply, Bath Council shared with the City Improvement Commissioners powers of pitching, paving, lighting, watching and scavenging. The division of such powers between the City, Bathwick and Walcot Commissioners and the administrative problems created by this were not addressed until 1851 and the resultant City Act itself generated further divisions which are discussed below in Section 3.2. The progress of foreign affairs had interfered with Bath's continued success as 34 premier British spa. The start of the war with France at the beginning of 1793, coupled with rising prices, exacerbated the effects of the trade depression which started at the end of the preceding year. Public confidence was shaken, the national economy declined, and the building boom in Bath came to a premature halt. Neale has linked the effects of the depression in Bath with the decline in its attractiveness to visitors. Using the level of toll collections made by the Improvement Commissioners he demonstrated that tolls only reached the 1792 levels in 1807/8 with a rise to 1820 of only 3% as compared with 15% 1789/93 (21). However, he broadly concurred with the opinion of A. B. Granville, medical travel writer of the 1830s and 1840s that the principal cause of the decline was the expansion of Bath during the 1788-92 boom (22). Granville observed that the turmoil and confinement of the large city that Bath had become were inappropriate for a health spa (23). This view was common at the turn of the century when, comparing Bath with his memories of it in 1780, a poet observed: " ... so mighty art thou grown, Thy head so large, thy trunk so swoln, Thy legs and arms so long and wide, And such an air of city pride; Thy sides so blackened by the smoke, ... thou art so Londoniz'd, So overbuilt and oversiz'd "(24). Similarly, modern historians have suggested that the decline of Bath from its premier position as resort for the fashionable began in the 1760s even as the Council was finally convinced of the financial viability of speculative building and the necessity of expansion (25). The fear of over development was a 35 recurring one although its early manifestations proved unfounded, John Wood remarked in 1765 that the citizens of Bath reacted against development as early as 1708, declaring, "0 Lord! Bath is undone; 'tis undone" (26). The appeal of Bath as a spa was its exclusivity and larger numbers of visitors, even if distinguished, compromised this. The Bath Journal recorded 510 such visitors in 1746 and 5341 in 1800 (27) which made the old regime, in which the Master of Ceremonies at the Assembly Rooms knew everyone and regulated their behaviour, an unmanageable task. Apart from the distinguished visitors middle-class families arrived, eager to partake in the public entertainments attended by the elite. In Smollett's opinion, formed after a visit in 1768, Bath had become, "the very centre of racket and dissipation - not peace, tranquillity and ease, so necessary to those who labour under bad health, weak nerves, and irregular spirits," (28) and was frequented by, "every upstart of fortune" with the result that, "a very inconsiderable proportion of genteel people are lost in a crowd of impudent plebians", an observation echoed in 1825 when an influential article, "The Bath Man", deplored the vulgarity of the city (29). The arrival of the crowds caused the elite to withdraw into the closed world of the private party. Granville also cited this, along with the high charges and indifferent treatment offered by Bath medical men, to be the main causes of the decline in visitors (30). Similarly, the local press acknowledged the deleterious effects of the, "exclusive, egotistical, eternal round of private parties" (31) on the popularity of the public entertainments. This was not exclusive to Bath but a progressive change in the social habits of the nation where increasingly formal and restricted gatherings replaced the public entertainments which characterised eighteenth century life (32). The permanent population of Bath had been swelled by the influx of workers 36 providing services for the visitors. As Neale has observed from the 1831 census, Bath housed half of the county's painters, one third of the pastry cooks and a quarter of the hatters though the city was inhabited by only one twelfth of the county's males over the age of 20 years (33). Similarly, members of the middle class including officers, their families and dependents began to retire to Bath which changed the nature of the social mix within the city. A publication as early as 1817 remarked that, "Bath is a sort of great monastery inhabited by single people, particularly superannuated females. No trade, no manufacture, no occupations of any sort, except that of killing time, the most laborious of all. Half of the inhabitants do nothing, the other half supply them with nothings" (34). According to a local historian of the 1860s, the last dwindling groups of socialites who normally spent a month in Bath before the London season ceased to do so by approximately 1840 (35). In 1841 Granville referred to, "your old codger and septugenarian, kept green by Bath air, Bath water and Bath whist," (36) as typical of the habitues of the Milsom St. circulating library. The Report of the Royal Commission of Inquiry into Municipal Corporations (1835) observed that Bath had significantly more permanent inhabitants than previously and that property had depreciated between 20 and 25%, "from several years back" (37). Local propagandists reported in 1841 that whole streets of houses formerly occupied by the wealthy, probably temporary residents, were taken over by mechanics and tradesmen on reduced rentals, whilst, "multitudes", were empty (38). In 1831 14% of the adult males in Bath were of the leisured and professional classes and this proportion was maintained in 1841; however, the labouring population declined from 19% to 15.5% suggesting an increase in craftsmen and retailers (39). Below these occupied classes were the drifting poor, numbering up to 20,000 per annum (40). The construction of the Great Western Railway (GWR) had not been an advantage to the city but had served to 37 undermine the coaching trade on which large central hotels like the "White Hart" and "Royal York" relied. It facilitated travel to London from the West Country rather than the reverse and accelerated the decline of the Quay area, as the siting of the railway station there attracted more itinerants and criminals who preyed on travellers. Bath developed as a retirement haven and accumulated a predominantly female population. Perceiving this as a deterrent to visitors, local guides claimed that this predominance was decreasing e.g. Meyler's guide for 1846 (41) noted that in 1821 there were 1.4 females per male and in 1841, 1.38 females per male. However, the underlying trend was for the predominance to increase and by 1861 there were 1.6 females per male which should be compared with the national figure in 1841 of 1.046 to appreciate its significance. Furthermore, this proportion increased to only 1.055 by 1881. Neale commented that high ratios of women in the retirement age bracket were resident and over half of the employed women in other age brackets were domestic servants (42). Such a preponderance was common in other spas, with Cheltenham having the reputation, "of possessing more spinsters and old maids, more widows and half-pay yellows from the Indus and the Ganges, together with lots of methodists and tee-totallers, than are necessary to render the place as dull as ditchwater" (43). In general terms, from an overall peak of approximately 54,000 (to the nearest thousand) in 1851, the population declined to 52,000 by 1891 (44). This represents a fate similar to that of a town uninvolved with leisure provision such as Macclesfield, although numbers there undulated at a level 20,000 below the figures for Bath. The massive tripling of the Birmingham population during the 1831-1891 period and the emergence of Southend-on-sea from hamlet in 1851 to 

recognised population centre of 3,000 in 1861 and town of 12,000 in 1891 reflect 38 the nineteenth century industrial and recreational developments of which Bath was not a part (45). However, as has been demonstrated by Graham Davis's work, the apparent 40% decline in population experienced by central Bath between 1851 and 1901 is countered by a doubling of the largely working class populations of Lyncombe and Widcombe and the villages of Twerton and Weston (46). Although the villages were not absorbed by Bath city until 1911 they were physically linked with Bath by the mid-nineteenth century by continuous residential building and emphasised the acquisition of a large working class population by the city. Even in Britain which had the largest percentage of its population living in towns of any in the world, Bath was a large urban centre, as a borough population of over 50,000 was typical for the average town dweller only by 1900 (47), but it had declined from being eleventh largest town in Great Britain in 1801 to twentieth by 1841 and thirty-fifth by 1871 (48). As Neale's researches have stressed, Bath had a politically active, skilled working-class, housed primarily in the parishes of St James, Lyncombe and Widcombe and parts of Walcot. Within the city as a whole approximately 40% of males over the age of 20 years were craftsmen or independent masters in small workshops (49). Heavy industrial manufacture was not important in the city's economy, although the Stothert family continued to succeed as iron founders (50). There was modest enterprise in shipbuilding with three vessels, the largest being 31 tons, having been positively identified as Bath built and, as Angus Buchanan has already observed, the city operated as a transport and communications centre from its earliest history (51). Contemporary opinion cited printing, coach building, cabinet making and brewing as important occupations (52). There were between 14-16 printers between 1848-1878 which included 5 newspapers and Pitman's enterprise which attained national importance, but the impact on the job market of all the 39 noted occupations was insignificant. A survey in 1869 confirmed that even the largest workshop only employed 35 people and the largest number in one room was twenty (53). The 1841 census showed that Bath's economy was centred on the domestic needs of residents and visitors. Table 1 shows occupations which employed more than one hundred males or females of over 20 years of age and, as an extension of Neale's work on the 1831 census, what proportion of the county's work force these figures represented. The figures were calculated from the 1841 census abstract of occupations for the county of Somerset, where the City of Bath's population of 38,304 represented 8.8% of the total for the county. This figure included only the city parishes designated in the 1590 charter which established the corporation, i.e. St James, St Michael, SS Peter and Paul, and part of Walcot. In 1835 Bathwick, Lyncombe and Widcombe and outlying sections of Walcot parishes were included in the city boundaries for municipal and parliamentary purposes. This created a population of 53,196 which included predominantly working-class areas in Lyncombe and Widcombe and middle-class areas in Bathwick and parts of outer Walcot.
