Domestic service was the biggest employer of workers overall, with females representing over four fifths of the total. Although males were occupied most popularly in labouring which was the second largest employer, almost half that number worked in domestic service, the second most popular job for the age group. Also, over half of the county's porters, errand boys and female lodging house keepers lived in Bath which supports the notion of a service economy operated by the working class, as do the relatively high figures for charwomen, seamstresses, dress-makers and milliners, the laundry trade, drapers and grocers. Bath's continued success as a health spa is indicated by the fact that it housed 24.4% of the county's physicians, surgeons and apothecaries and 26.3% of its nurses. The city's 7th - 9th and 13th most populous occupations were related to building, maintenance and furnishing, the most significant figure being that of the cabinet makers and upholsterers which provided 39.9% of the county's work force in those trades. Coach making accounted for 36.9%, printing 31.3% and brewing 17.8% of the county's employees in those skills, but were not major employers in the city. Similarly, Bath employed over 30% of the county's coach men, guards and post boys, staymakers and straw bonnet and hat makers. Only coach making, with 97 employees, and the coach men, guards and post boys group which involved 95 persons, approached the threshold chosen for this analysis. The total numbers of independent individuals both male and female when added to the residual totals of the adult population, who were not included 42 in the occupational analysis, represent 8.9% of the county totals for this class of unoccupied resident. This varies only by 0.1% from the proportion of the city's population to that of the county. This suggests two possibilities: that a significant number of visitors continued to frequent Bath and that the leisured residents were at least moderately affluent, thus the disproportionate development of trade persisted despite the city's loss of social cachet. It would be perverse to describe Bath as an industrial city, yet it had a vocal artisan population which, by the start of the nineteenth century, caused it to become a centre of Radicalism. The people were praised by the Northern Star Chartist newspaper for their love of liberty and prevailing democratic spirit (55). Similarly, Henry Vincent the Chartist orator observed that, "Radicalism was never so honoured in any town or city in the nation" (56), see Section 2.2. Reform in 1832 made Bath one of the most democratic representative boroughs with one in three of all adult males obtaining the suffrage as opposed to the average in the 1832-1869 period of only one in five (57). Thus it was the change in Bath's social structure coupled with the national popularity of reform which caused the city not only to re-elect the Whig Palmer, but also to choose John Arthur Roebuck the ultra-Radical in the election of 1832. Roebuck was invited to stand for Bath on the recommendation of Joseph Hume the Radical MP and was selected in preference to the traditional Whig, Hobhouse, who was the third candidate. Roebuck was a challenger of aristocratic and imperial control and was to become an early champion of Chartism (58). In the early 1830s, before the "physical force" mentality split reforming politics, Roebuck appeared a natural choice for the bulk of the tradesmen voters and reforming intelligensia alike. However, such a representative was contrary to the received self-image of the city. The local Tory press provided the clearest description of the traditional 43 image of Bath, describing it as the chosen resort of, "polished manners ... rank, wit and learning" which had regretably merged with, "malignant falsehood ... (and) nauseous radicalism" (59). Movement Party rhetoric was brought to Bath as Radical opinion acted temporarily in accord with middle-class liberalism and although Roebuck lost his seat in 1837 he regained it in 1841 against the tide of Conservative popularity. He distanced himself from the Chartists over their emphasis on the importance of social reform and espousal of physical force and remained MP until 1847 and the waning of Radical influence. Graham Davis pointed out the error in earlier researches conducted by Hope, Wadsworth, Kite and Neale who highlighted the Radical element of Bath to 1850 and dismissed the rest of the nineteenth century as one dominated by Conservatism, on the basis that it was the 1890s before Conservatism gained dominant strength. The genteel image projected was out of kilter with the reality of a society still peopled by a 75% majority of the working class (60). The Radical revival during the 1850s, analysed below in Part 3, confirms this refutation. See Appendix 3 for additional detail on Bath's parliamentary representation. Bath was a victim of its own success and became a city at odds with the concept of a fashionable retreat. In 1843 the concerned gentry of Bath met to form a Committee to discuss how to extend the attractions of the city and improve publicity in London. During the committee meeting it was stated that Bath had lost, "caste", as it became a city of residence and had lost its appeal to visitors of the calibre of princes, war heroes and statesmen who had visited within the lifetimes of the committee members (61). Bath had grown out of its former charm and was associated with an ancien regime that no longer pertained in the new Europe. The revolutions of the late eighteenth century and the growth of the reform movement had brought change to the self-image and pleasures of the aristocratic elite. Also, the conclusion of the French Wars permitted tourists of 44 the upper and middle classes to visit continental spas. Gamblers were attracted to Baden-Baden, Hamburg and Monaco; those taking the waters for dietary purposes frequented Schwalbach or Kissingen (62). Although some aristocrats favoured Harrogate as an alternative to Bath; Wiesbaden, Marienbad and Karlsbad were chosen by the most stylish (63). Instead of Bath being the only resort acceptable for the elite, a multiplicity of choice became available. Apart from the exotic allure of the Continent, the cults of Romanticism and the Picturesque encouraged exploration of rustic retreats and more dramatic scenery than that provided by Bath, similarly, the developing interest in sea bathing caused visitors to seek coastal resorts. Scarborough and Brighton were reputed to be the most crowded resorts by the 1860s (64). Brighton's population increased from almost 7.5 thousand in 1801 to over 69.5 thousand in 1851 (65) enjoying the highest growth rate of any town in the country (66). Jeremy suggested that by 1815 even the middle classes were seeking entertainment at other spas and that the general economic decline of the first half of the nineteenth century also contributed to the deepening depression in Bath (67). This should not be over stated as Bath received an unprecedented number of royal visitors between 1817-1830 and continued to expand despite rival attractions and the decline of traditional public entertainments (68). Although Bath was still acknowledged to have superior facilities and was frequented by the county aristocracy (69), Cheltenham had become the most fashionable spa over the first thirty years of the century, with its cold saline and iron springs famed for their laxative effects, but it was eclipsed by Leamington in the 1840s, despite the lack of public entertainments there (70). Cheltenham's success in creating an alternative to Bath stemmed from George III's visit in 1788 when he sought a more restrained location for a cure but, despite the exploitation 45 of six springs, the royal patronage was not sustained and the spa was in decline by the 1830s, as the town constructed its grandest pump room, the domed Pittville complex (71). Some depression was common to all English spas during this period (72) and the decline in the numbers and quality of visitors was perceived to be a major economic problem by contemporaries. Propagandists such as the editor of the Original Bath Guide tempered optimistic remarks concerning Bath's prosperity and appeal by admitting that the balls were not staged regularly and, as the city could no longer attract eminent performers, the subscription concerts had been discontinued (73). Anonymous polemical writers published bitter complaints e.g. in 1840 "Lud Hudibras" described the city as deserted and questioned that, during the previous winter, "was there scarcely a day when a cannon ball might not have been fired right up Milsom Street (the principal shopping street) without the probability of doing any grievous bodily harm ... save perhaps to some luckless shopkeeper who for the want of better employment may have been standing at his shop door." (74). This remark was not original which diminished the validity of the pamphleteer's message. It was a re-working of a reference to the quietness of Bath out of season in the early eighteenth century. The original quotation involved charging a, "culverin with grapeshot", and firing it down Stall Street with the only likely targets being, "a turnspit dog or a pig" (75). A less alarmist observation from William Clark, mayor of the unreformed corporation from November 1832, declared that the city was as successful in trade as nine out of ten cities and better off than four out of six (76). His analysis of the situation was that the city's economy had changed as more people were in trade and living in the city than at the turn of the century when the bulk of the shops would close in the low summer season. In the 1830s and 1840s 46 shops were able to open all year round because of demand from permanent residents. As Pimlott observed, Bath continued to flourish as it was recognised as a town with a spa instead of the reverse (77). The urban infra-structure had grown from the beginning of the eighteenth century and provided the base for Bath's revival in the last quarter of the nineteenth century. However, in the 1840s the loss of fashionable visitors was deplored in the official and unofficial press, the attitude of the shopkeepers being cited as a cause of the decline. "Lud Hudibras" blamed the, "vainglorious shopocracy" of tradesmen, for alienating visitors by their contemptuous service (78) and for sabotaging the public entertainments by not attending them. A provocative exchange of letters in 1841 (79) also criticised shopkeepers for being too proud to serve. Both these sources also blamed the increasingly religious atmosphere in the city for the decline in visitors. "Pulpit anathematization" (80) of concerts, races, balls, theatre and even horticultural shows occurred in the crusade against amusements. Bath was declared to be a, "poverty struck, priest ridden city" (81). This is reflected in the activities of the Simeon Trust, whose scheme for the purchasing of advowsons to further the Evangelical cause was particularly successful within the city. Bath Abbey with its satellite churches was the most distinguished asset secured by the Trust and was obtained even though Simeon feared his, "poor pittance" would be swallowed up by the effort (82). Beggars were reported as having responded to the increasingly religious atmosphere and a local journal noted that a letter from a beggar of Leamington to one of Cheltenham stated, "Well Jack we have used up these places pretty well. We must go to Bath it is a fine place for the pious dodge" (83). This unsubstantiated account is probably apocryphal and invented to illustrate the growing concern about Bath's reputation as an excessively religious and 47 charitable city. As a topical poem observed, "For begging here a perfect trade is - supported chiefly by the ladies" (84). Females were in the majority, but this preponderance alone had not attracted beggars who had been present since the medieval period and increased in numbers with the increase in rich visitors in the eighteenth century. The Rev. Earle observed in his history of 1864 that, "the dens of Holloway filled with beggars" as the Squares and Crescents filled with the affluent. The beggars, "watched the visitors who were their prey, and eluded the Corporation who were their natural enemies" (85). A history of Bath 

completed in 1801 stated that only a small number of lower class individuals lived in Bath and those were well known, which operated as a powerful check on them and prevented misdemeanours (86). Even allowing for his definition of "lower class" to exclude the respectable working class his observation excluded comment on the itinerant poor who would not have been known to the higher classes which he believed constituted the chief part of the population. As the streets were, "thronged with beggars" (87) the Monmouth Society was formed in 1805 by a group of Anglican residents who wished to speed the arrest of the undeserving and the relief of the rest. In 1838 whilst Jerom Murch was pastor of Trim St. Unitarian Chapel, see Section 1.3, he preached against the, "Unchristian spirit in Bath" (88). As a Unitarian, Murch was opposed to the Evangelical emphasis on original sin and the rejection of high culture. He observed that, "It is now the fashion to be Evangelical" (89) and that apart from a partiality for Bishops and, "a few badges of Popery ... the members of the Long Parliament would find no city more congenial with their tastes" (90). The religious census of 1851 revealed that Bath was better provided for in terms of church sittings than any other city of comparable size in the country. Horace Mann's calculations required provision for 58% of the local populace and Bath provided for 61.1%. Although 48 Colchester provided for 73.2% and Wakefield for 70.9% both these towns had less than half the population of Bath. Similarly, York provided for 65.1% yet had only two thirds of Bath's population. In Bath 63.2% of the provision was Anglican and the remaining 36.8% was provided by the seventeen other sects in the city (91). Inglis's index of attendance, which calculated an average of total attendances as a percentage of the population, registered 49.7 for towns with populations of over 10,000 and 71.4 for small towns and rural areas. Bath's index of attendance was 79.1 which was above that for small towns and was only exceeded amongst large towns by Exeter at 84.5 and Colchester at 89.5, all three towns being, in Inglis's words, "scarcely touched by manufacture" (92). Bath may therefore be described as unusually dominated by religious sensibility, even in a period when religious observance was an important feature in the life of the artisan class and above. The contrast between this new preoccupation and the city's previous persona as vortex of fashion emphasised the impression of sobriety. However, it was not permitted to suppress Bath's entertainments. An example of the local antagonism between the Evangelical hierarchy and the supporters of traditional Bath public entertainments was the brisk pamphleteering of the first three months of 1844. The Rev. John East, Rector of St Michael's Church, had published a sermon against playhouses and dramatic literature declaring theatres to be of heathen origin, a danger to unescorted females and, "strongly marked ... with almost every variety of evil" (93). Residents and churchmen alike published their criticisms of his views (94). It is important to balance the popular image of Bath as a sedate, pious city with the fact that the theatre remained open and was rebuilt in 1862 after a serious fire. One opponent of East noted that he witnessed immoral assignations in the chancel of the Abbey during services just as frequently as at the theatre but with the advantage for the participants that meetings could take place under the cover of church attendance 49 (95). Similarly, satirical poems of the 1830s depict crowded streets and theatrical events such as the Dramatic Fete involving crowds revelling until dawn (96). In the spirit of the Evangelical revival and the predominating ethic of utility the elites of the city sought to establish a new reputation based on improvement and moral regeneration. Conscience dominated the psyche of the town by the 1830s instead of being kept at bay by the hell hounds of Satan, as a satirical poet had suggested in 1773 (97). In Jeremy's view the middle class elite and their comparatively plebian rule replaced Nash's, "conservatoire of good manners" (98). Alternatively, this may be viewed as the high Whig rule of private compromise and public strictures against the prevailing tide of easy vulgarity being replaced by an ethos of strict morality and intellectual rigour developed to confront the urgent demands for improvement in a changed world. It is important not to overstate the extent of Bath's decline. Bath did not cease to trade or entertain visitors in the first half of the nineteenth century. Temporary improvements such as the Assembly Rooms attendance for 1835 showed almost a doubling of subscribers for card assemblies and balls (99) from 70 to 135, and 289 to 475 respectively and the guides were still able to describe the resort as prosperous which it was, though shunned by high society (100). In similar vein the 1837 winter season was described as one of the most prosperous ever known in the city with vacant houses a rarity, the streets full of company (101) and the subscription ball of the following spring the most splendid ever hosted and attracting 700 guests (102). The major growth area of Bath was recognised as that of a city of permanent residence, the city being described as the, "Cradle of Old Age" (103), and the best city for the retirement of individuals, "past the meridian of life" (104). From 1801 Bath was marketed as a place without trade and commerce, but with 50 decorous entertainments and cheap provisions (105). Living in style in Bath was claimed to cost one third less than, "mere comfort", in Brighton (106), yet it still stocked, "the refinements rather than the necessities of life" (107). Bath's shopocracy was not driven out of business on a significant scale by the decline in numbers of visitors as the residents and shoppers from the surrounding rural areas and small towns continued to buy in the city. However, to encourage visitors and increase the use of the spa, in 1830 the Hot Baths were refitted by the unreformed council, according to a local historian to a, "magnificent standard. unparalleled in any city in Europe; whether as to taste, elegance, convenience or useful adaptation", and as a gesture to the needs of the inhabitants as opposed to the visitors, the poor were allowed to use the Hot Bath for 6d, a third of the standard fee (108). The refurbishment appeared to have been successful with income from the Baths increasing over three fold from £471 14s 7d over the year 1823/4, to a high level of £1,507 19s in 1831 which declined only to £1,365 17s in 1833 (109). This compared well with the figure of £998 9s id taken in 1805. The Pump Room was leased out in the early years of the nineteenth century but civic control was re-established. Figures for takings in 1823/4 almost equalled the Baths' figures for 1805 at £985 19s 10d but the total more than halved to £448 us 10d in 1833 and continued to drop as the attendance at public venues declined. Although the Baths' takings did not fall below £1,000 per year and experienced a slight increase in 1840, costs negated any benefit and caused a £6 9s lld loss over the three years before the council relinquished control (110). The Baths and Pump Room were leased out to private managers for a trial period of three years in September 1840. By 1846, and after having to renegotiate a cheaper lease because of low receipts (111), the lessees Messrs Green and Simms were commended by a local writer for having brought the, "highest degree of luxury 51 and elegance", to the facilities (112). This was supported by the account of a German diarist recorded in 1850 which favourably compared the Baths with any facilities he had seen in Germany (113). The council also undertook expensive building works in the early 1830s to increase the attractions of the centre. These included a controversial remodelling of the Abbey despite councillors claiming that "restoration" was their, "motto and polar star" (114). After the municipal reform of 1835, incoming ultra-Radical hatter, Alderman James Crisp, a proponent of economy and retrenchment policies, castigated the developments as, "useless and unnecessary buildings". The outgoing mayor George Norman, a successful surgeon, defended the expenditure as valid investment to provide a city capable of providing a substantial rate when required (115). This exchange typified the traditional view of the council's responsibilities for improvement. Elitist developments for the privileged few would be undertaken on the understanding that enrichment of the city at the highest level would percolate down to the less worthy inhabitants at the base of the social pyramid. Although activities such as the opening of the Royal Victoria Park in 1830, the first Victoria Park in the country, might be construed as a more enlightened form of provision, it was instigated by private initiative and supported by councillors principally to provide some summer entertainment for visitors and enhance the city (116). The provision of temporary labour which benefited the poor was purely coincidental. The lack of interest in improving the working class areas was illustrated by the debate concerning the building of an additional bridge in order that respectable inhabitants of Widcombe need not travel through, "the filthy, odious Dolemeads", a working class area which developed adjacent to the juncture of the River Avon and the Kennet and Avon Canal open from 1802, was 52 prone to flooding and locally referred to as "Mud Island" (117), before crossing the bridge to the south of the city. Similarly, the police force was consolidated and reorganised on the metropolitan pattern, re-emphasising the commitment to protection of property as opposed to the provision of water and drainage for the majority (118). A local historian Austin King, writing with the benefit of hindsight in 1888, described the eighteenth century experience in Bath as being a phase of unreality and artificially high pressure towards the end of which the city had itself begun to establish a broader base (119). The permanent residents which replaced the floating population of visitors included, according to King, "men of large minds" who had, "real and intelligent interest in municipal affairs" (120). The reform of the municipal corporations permitted the Dissenting and largely Radical sector of this reservoir of enthusiasm to be tapped. Such new men were not restricted by the hegemony of local landed patricians, a disabling situation high-lighted by D. Cannadine's research (121). Although landowners in the rural hinterland were able to hinder municipal projects which impinged on their property, their political influence was negligible. The Marquis of Bath was the only aristocrat who had exercised direct political influence over the Bath electorate and this had been lost after the Municipal Reform Act. Lord Manvers' extensive holdings in the city did not tempt him to spend time in Bath and influence its political or economic life; neither did the Duke of Cleveland's ownership of Bathwick cause him to interfere with local politics. Similarly, the city did not depend upon a sole manufactory or a small number of large businesses and their proprietors to sustain the urban economy, but housed a large number of small enterprises which prevented domination by local entrepreneurs. The various strata within the middle class dominated the local political arena and conducted their power broldng without the pressure of unelected noble influence. However, this 53 freedom was negated by sharp antagonisms generated within the bourgeoisie and upper middle class which resulted in the recruitment of lower class or central government support to further their causes and thus restricted council independence. Such impositions, were not envisaged in 1835 when the newly elected council was expected to enjoy a novel freedom of action to carry out the harmonious wishes of Radical reformers. 05

Plate 2: Sir Jerom Murch, 1894 

(Photograph taken courtesy of the Victoria Art Gallery) 64 1.3 Sir Jerom Murch: his background and significance in Bath society 1833-1862 By the last decade of the nineteenth century Sir Jerom Murch had become the city's most potent symbol and personification of municipal idealism: his contribution to local government politics was imbued with the sacred motivation typical of the national civic ideal established in the 1860s and 1870s. His sense of mission was rendered peculiarly suited to civic service because of his Unitarian principles. A fundamental belief in toleration and his acceptance of a changing definition of truth equipped him to adapt to the dynamics of a local government role which was in the first phase of its evolution to premier engine of reform. In order to assess the significance of his civic role it is necessary to trace the establishment of his position in Bath society, his networks of influence and the position of Unitarianism within Bath which was an urban bastion of Anglicanism. He was born in Honiton, Devonshire, on 29th October 1807. His family was entrenched in Protestant Dissent, the paternal line being descended from Huguenot refugees. Samuel Smiles in his history of Huguenot settlements noted that Murch was a common example of a refugee family name within the Flemish and French communities in Honiton and Colyton, the latter being the home of Jerom's mother Ann Burnard who was herself the descendent of one of the clergy ejected from the Anglican church in 1662. The emigres established their traditional trades which included the manufacture of "bone-lace", mining, fish preserving and metal work, the last occupation being undertaken by Jerom's family who were silversmiths (1). He was of the sixth generation of his branch of the family whose ancestor, John or Jonas Murch, arrived in Plymouth before 1648 and served on Plymouth Council before his death in 1723. The family had moved to Honiton by 1739 and diversified their trade into clockmaking. Jerom 65 Murch's father, William, ran an ironmongery in Honiton as he had been brought up by a great-uncle who was a brazier and tinsmith. It was in this business rather than the clockmaking undertaken by his half-brother Matthew that Jerom worked after being withdrawn from school at an early age. As a member of a large family with five step- and six full siblings the teenage Murch pursued his own education, attended art lessons and organised local improvement classes in modern languages (2). Murch's grandfather, another Jerom, was a staunch member of Honiton's early Baptist congregation and, in company with his son, was on the rebuilding committee for the new Bridge Meeting House in 1794. The Honiton Baptists had been revivified in the early eighteenth century by the inspirational figure of Jerom Maynard, another Huguenot descendent and monied serge manufacturer who was related to the Murch family by marriage. He arrived in Honiton in 1715, preached free of charge to the people and financed the building of the original meeting house in 1737 (3). The Murch family had taken the name Jerom with the unusual omission of the final "e" as a mark of respect to Maynard (4) and some were influenced towards an acceptance of Unitarian beliefs by his support of the Arian Christology. At nineteen years of age Murch had decided to train for the ministry at the General Baptist Academy in Newington Green, London, under the supervision of the Rev. James Gilchrist as he was not at this stage committed to a Unitarian theology (5). However, his predisposition to this and an aversion to the Calvinistic preoccupations of the Particular Baptists, prevented him from attending the prestigious Baptist College at Stepney, where his father's cousin William Harris Murch DD, who was also from Honiton, became the newly appointed third president in the same year that Murch left home (6). In a 66 subsequent history Murch has been identified as one of the two distinguished students to attend the academy although he attended only a part of the three year course because of the religious doubts and resignation of his tutor. Murch received temporary instruction in the homes of Baptist ministers before he enrolled as one of the first intake of students at the fledgling and controversial University of London in 1828. Murch obtained his place through the intervention of the Welsh iron-master Sir Josiah Guest (7), who was MP for Honiton 1826-1831 and then for the new seat of Merthyr Tydfil, and was also a shareholder in the university and thus able to nominate students and negotiate lower fees for them. Murch studied a desultory mixture of junior classics, mathematics and museum studies but as the university was unable to award degrees until 1836 when it became the awarding body of University College, he was unable to graduate before he left to take up his first pastorate, which was for the Unitarian meeting at Diss, Norfolk, in the summer of 1829. The following year Murch married Ann Meadows Taylor, seven years his senior and third daughter of Meadows Taylor, head of a wealthy Unitarian family related to the Martineaus of Norwich, and therefore to both James the Unitarian divine and his sister Harriet the writer and political economist. Through the Taylor family Murch became familiar with the intellectual circle of the late Anna Laetitia Barbauld, protege of Joseph Priestley, educationalist, writer and poetess who had also been the wife of a previous Unitarian pastor at Diss, and who had died in 1825. Murch was keen to promote the importance of female contributions to public life and later wrote a book on Mrs Barbauld's achievements and those of other literary and scientific Englishwomen (8). Also, his support of two female candidates for places on the first Bath School Board caused him to lose his own seat, see Section 4.4.2 below. Whilst in Diss, Murch also attended sermons of all the noted preachers in the area to improve his effectiveness in the pulpit. This 67 essentially eclectic approach and commitment to effective communication were to become principal strengths in his future civic career. By 1833 Murch's ambition, and to a lesser degree his ill health which created a desire to move closer to Honiton, caused him to seek a new position. Whilst in Diss he claimed he had, "long wished to have more society and to be in a larger sphere of usefulness than this neighbourhood affords" (9). An opportunity had arisen in Bath on the resignation of the Rev. Joseph Hunter, pastor of Trim St Chapel for the previous 34 years. As an antiquarian and archivist of national repute, Hunter had been invited to work in London where he later became Senior Assistant Keeper at the Public Record Office (10). However, he had not improved the fortunes of Trim St and dwindling congregations had reduced his income to a level at which it had to be subsidised out of the half yearly collection (11). In Murch's words, Hunter was, "too quiet, thoughtful and ... heterodox, to be a popular preacher", as he avoided all disputation and proselytizing and offered no clear spiritual lead to his congregation (12). The position was therefore to provide Murch with a challenging apprenticeship to public life. Murch was looked upon favourably by the Trustees of Trim St as he was reputed to be an adequate preacher and his supporters stressed the value of his wife as an heiress, whose money would free Murch from the necessity of running a school to supplement his income (13). Unfortunately for them, the Taylor funds were not available to the Murch family at this time and Murch's health problems proved to be so significant as to precipitate an early retirement, shortly after he had established himself as a leading minister in the West Country. However, the impecunious Murch was accepted and arrived in the autumn of 1833 to take up his post. 68 Trim St Chapel, built in 1795 as a Unitarian meeting house, was officially designated Presbyterian because of remaining legal restictions on Unitarianism but the congregation had accepted Unitarian theology by the 1780s and was the direct descendent of the first Dissenting congregation in the city which formed in 1672. By the start of the nineteenth century it had become an elitist group, for example, Hunter had been against a popular preaching initiative and addressed himself solely to the respectable classes, although some of the congregation took part in forming a local missionary association in 1824 which later merged with the British and Foreign Unitarian Association (BFUA). Murch wished to attract the lower classes whilst he recognised that it was the wealthy members who enabled the chapel to remain solvent (14). The strength of the Evangelical movement in Bath produced a particularly hostile theological climate for Unitarianism. Bath was notably well provided with well attended churches. According to the 1851 religious census, Anglicans controlled 55 out of the 111 churches in Bath, the various Methodist groups accounted for 30, the Baptists 10 and the Independents 5, with the Rev. Jay's Argyle St Chapel housing the most numerous Dissenting congregation. The Unitarians had one chapel providing 300 sittings, the same number as the Friends and Moravians. Attendance at the morning service showed that 175 attended the Unitarian chapel whereas the Friends attracted only 47 and the Moravians were overfull at 390. In contrast the combined Anglican congregation for that morning was 16.4 thousand (15). Murch arrived in Bath at a time of worsening conflict between the Church and Dissent and also the bulk of the Dissenting body, particularly Congregationalists, and Unitarians. The Manchester Socinian controversy of 1824, concerning the rights of Unitarians to hold property under trust deeds drawn up for orthodox 69 congregations, had been eclipsed in importance by the Lady Hewley Charity case, the eiwision on which was against the Unitarians in 1833, the year in which Murch arrived in Bath. The situation was only resolved in 1844 by Peel's Dissenting Chapels Act, one year before Murch was obliged to resign his post through ill health, therefore, his ministry was dominated by the struggle. Murch lobbied MPs and arranged petitions to parliament and also, his most important Unitarian publication describing the histories of the Presbyterian and General Baptist churches in the West of England which was completed in 1835 was an important piece of propaganda for the Unitarian cause as it reinforced the claims of the congregations to their property (16). As part of this conflict, Murch entered into public disputation in the Bath press with the Trinitarian Bible Society, set up in 1832 in opposition to the original British and Foreign Bible Society largely because of the admission of "Socinians" who were unacceptable to Evangelicals. The Secretary of the new group, Edwin Caulfield, encapsulated the prevailing attitude of his subscribers and the majority of Bath residents to Unitarianism when he replied to Murch's offer to explain his beliefs that, "Not a single member ... could endure to listen to sentiments which compromise the Lord's honour and their eternal safety ... I ought to mourn over, to compassionate and to pray for you!". It was in the Unitarian press that the widespread success of Evangelicalism in Bath was not only on account of the general dissemination of its principles but also because of, "the large number of unoccupied, we will not say vacant minds", in the city, noted as a middle-classs retirement haven (17). This antagonism acted as a spur to develop Murch's role within the community beyond that of other ministers within the Non-Conformist body. 70 During his ministry, Murch campaigned to improve public knowledge about Unitarianism as hostility increased, for as he observed in a published sermon of 1835, "the clouds be gathering for a tempest" (18). He and his fellow members of the "Frigid Zone" of religion (19) were religous pariahs and regarded as heretics in the enthusiastic atmosphere of Evangelicalism, and according to a local sermon were more to be dreaded than the cholera (20). Pupils at the day school for girls run by the chapel were claimed to have been poached by, "means highly improper", employed by members of the established church and because of this harassment, after being full with 70 pupils in 1840, attendance was reduced to less than 50% by 1848 (21). However, despite the antipathy of the town, Murch increased the Trim St congregation by over eight fold during his early ministry, from an average of 20-30 in 1833 to 250 in 1834, which however, fell back to 150-200 by 1844 but included the sought after young men (22) as well as the ladies who Murch referred to as, "the great preponderance of bonnets" (23). The experience of reviving the fortunes of the chapel and functioning within its administrative structure constituted part of Murch's political apprenticeship, during which he campaigned successfully for greater congregational democracy despite the unwillingness of the Trustees to relinquish control (24). Murch's Unitarianism embodied a commitment to education, the pursuit of truth through reason and also to tolerance which necessitated his involvement in political and cultural endeavours in the city outside his religious duties. This involvement, which as endorsed by Dawson, Dale and Crosskey in Birmingham in the 1860s became the essence of the civic gospel, served as another aspect of Murch's political training. One of his earliest public speeches in Bath was at a meeting concerned with the reform of the Irish Church, where as the only cleric sharing a platform with local Radicals and Whig reformers he moved a resolution 71 supporting the right of the state to deal with church property (25). Although not as vehement as the principal speaker, Col. William Napier, historian and veteran of the Peninsular War and brother of Sir Charles noted for his career in Sind who was also active in local politics, Murch was criticised for his, "bold declaration of war against tithe property" (26). He had forseen that, "no small degree of odium" (27) would result from his public involvement in politics but he continued to attend and speak at Radical reform meetings. Predictably Murch opposed church rates but unlike the majority of traditional Unitarians, who still hoped for an eventual reconciliation with Anglicanism, he also supported disestablishment, and referred to the church as an, "ancient, unbending, extravagant, anathamatizing woman", in a metaphorical marriage with the people, that he visualised as a, "modern, improving, economical but rather refractory gentleman" (28). Murch supported the Maynooth grant in 1838 in response to the circulation of anti-catholic speakers, before the more significant action against the grant in 1843 when Peel moved to increase it. The disestablishment movement which gathered pace after the emancipation of the catholics, had stimulated provincial sessions of anti-catholic rhetoric such as the closed meeting at the White Lion public house in Bath, which informed adult male listeners of the supposed depravity of the establishment at Maynooth (29). The following year, the city was visited by Hugh McNeile, Irish leader of the Liverpool and Birkenhead Evangelical clergy and archetypal representative of militant Protestantism. F. Neal's researches have shown how McNeile nourished sectarian violence in Liverpool and led the campaign which defeated the Liberals there after their temporary gains of the mid 1830s (30). Neal commented that work remained to be done to gauge the extent of McNeile's speaking tours and was only able to indicate that reciprocal arrangements of speakers were made in Lancashire, therefore the meetings at Bath are indicative of a wider scale of 72 action (31). Murch attended the main meeting which featured McNeile but as speeches from the floor were vetoed, his riposte was in the form of an open letter to the citizens in support of the catholic cause (32) and a speech delivered at a mainly working-class rally for all denominations which was denounced in the Tory press as a, "wretched concern", attended by Catholics and, "the very refuse of Bath Radicals", with only the odd decent Protestant (33). By the mid-1840s, Murch led the Bath Liberals and directed their policy to a significant extent. In common with the most prominent Unitarians of the period, like James Martineau and William Johnson Fox who were noted spokesmen (34), Murch supported the Anti-Corn Law League. It was he who met Cobden and Bright on their arrival in Bath for a public meeting on 4th December 1845 and was able to inform them that Peel had agreed to repeal the Corn Laws (35). Murch shared a platform with the two principal speakers and local Radicals including Councillors Hunt and Gordon. His speech, which concentrated on the importance of light, air and space as well as cheap food, with all perceived as non-party issues, formed a parallel with his support for the Health of Towns Association. His commitment to freedom of action and tolerance is further illustrated by his support for the abolition of the death penalty, a popular cause amongst reformers in the 1840s (36). His public denial of support for Roebuck, cited by the MP as a prime cause of the Radical defeat in the election of 1847 emphasised Murch's importance. At the initial Liberal Selection Committee meeting on 22nd May 1847, Murch had withdrawn support for Roebuck (37), as had Councillors Willson Brown and Norman, because of Roebuck's antipathy to Whig policy. This view was supported by a large minority of the meeting, their mood being summed up by a Baptist minister who observed that, "the body of 1841 is there but the spirit has 73 fled", in reference to the increasingly unsuitable behaviour of Roebuck after his return to the seat in 1841 (38). Roebuck's denunciation of Murch on the hustings led to exchanges of letters in the local press, where Murch defended his position against Roebuck's, "groundless, unmanly attack" (39) whilst convalescing away from the city. Condemnation of Murch who was, "brooding over imaginary evils like a second Don Quixote", according to a Radical correspondent, accelerated to accusations of dishonourable desertion of the Bath Liberals, of which he was the acknowledged leader (40). Unitarian rectitude and abhorrence of violence allied Murch with the Whigs and necessarily distanced him from Roebuck whose support within the city was sacrificed through the violent excesses of his political style. Apart from religious and political campaigns, Murch was closely associated with educational and intellectual enterprises within the commmunity. Besides the chapel school his major involvements were with the Mechanics Institute and the Bath Royal Literary and Scientific Institution (BRLSI). Unitarianism was intimately connected with the Mechanics Institute movement as Birkbeck, who was the co-founder of the first institute in London in 1823 after his experiences at Anderson's Institute Glasgow, was inspired originally by a visit to the Birmingham Brotherly Society. This group was founded in 1796 as a development of the 1789 Sunday Society of Joseph Priestley's Unitarian church and included the Birmingham Artisan's Library as part of the initiative (41). The Institutes were perceived by Murch and fellow Unitarians to be symbols of religious and civil liberty (42) and he became connected with the Bath group soon after his arrival in the city (43). Along with Shenstone, a Liberal alderman and Keene the proprietor of the Liberal Bath Journal Murch was part of the main trio of middle class supporters of the Mechanics' Institute in Bath. 74 Shenstone had been the promoter of the council's Education Committee to investigate educational provision for the under-14s, a novel scheme which was only accepted after much opposition in council and achieved little. Murch helped with administration and lectured at the Institute e.g. on geology and English literature (44) and aimed to appeal to young students of the labouring classes. Despite such middle-class efforts, numbers of working men declined as their basic literacy levels were too low to benefit from the lectures. Rival establishments like the "General Instruction Society" could not have gained support if the Mechanics Institute had fulfilled its role more effectively. The rival society operated as a Tory/Anglican enterprise to counter the secular appeal of the Institute and received financial suport from leading Tories such as Powerscourt, Bath's MP (45). It was reported that Bath's Mechanics' Institute was one of the most legitimate of its class in the country as originally it was financed and attended by the class it sought to benefit (46). By 1831 it was claimed that not 1 in 10 members could be classed as journeymen mechanics, however in 1841, 70 of the 158 adult members were industrial employees and 52 master tradesmen were also members so the working classes did provide the majority of support for the enterprise. The rest of the membership ranged from medical men, those engaged in law and architects to shopkeepers and servants. The only clergyman involved apart from Murch was the Rev. T. # 1959 Studebaker: Throwing the baby out with the bath water

[September 10, 2021](https://www.indieauto.org/2021/09/)[Steve](https://www.indieauto.org/author/steve/)[Fake Design](https://www.indieauto.org/category/fake-design/)14

[![Image 3](https://i0.wp.com/www.indieauto.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/06/Ad-Indie-Auto-subscribe-2-col-col.png?fit=685%2C106&ssl=1)](https://www.indieauto.org/contact/free-newsletter/)

[![Image 4: 1959 and 1955 Studebaker rooflines](https://i0.wp.com/www.indieauto.org/wp-content/uploads/2015/05/1959-and-1955-Studebaker-rooflines-col.cov_.png?resize=678%2C381&ssl=1)](https://www.indieauto.org/2021/09/10/1959-studebaker-throwing-the-baby-out-with-the-bath-water/1959-and-1955-studebaker-rooflines-col-cov/)

[](mailto:?subject=1959%20Studebaker%3A%20Throwing%20the%20baby%20out%20with%20the%20bath%20water&body=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.indieauto.org%2F2021%2F09%2F10%2F1959-studebaker-throwing-the-baby-out-with-the-bath-water%2F "Send this article to a friend")[](javascript:window.print() "Print this article")

_(EXPANDED FROM 5/22/2015)_

The 1959 Studebaker Lark’s design was initially so successful that it was described by historian Robert Ebert as a “miracle” ([2013](https://www.indieauto.org/2013/10/26/champion-of-the-lark-harold-churchill-and-the-presidency-of-studebaker-packard-1956-1961/), p. 55). Studebaker-Packard Corporation, which was on the verge of liquidating its automotive operations, suddenly found itself with a hot-selling car and — for one year — no direct competition from the Big Three. Alas, unlike the Rambler, Studebaker’s prospects quickly fizzled with the arrival of compacts from General Motors, Ford and Chrysler. Why?

[![Image 5: 1960 Studebaker Lark ingress](https://i0.wp.com/www.indieauto.org/wp-content/uploads/2015/05/1960-Stude-door-small.png?resize=279%2C363&ssl=1)](http://www.oldcarbrochures.org/)

_In 1960 Studebaker used a six-foot model to show how flat floors and tall doors were an advantage ([Old Car Brochures](http://www.oldcarbrochures.org/))._

Let’s start by acknowledging that the 1959 Studebaker’s designers had three big — and perhaps insurmountable — challenges:

**Body architecture —** The basic Studebaker body dated back to 1953, so did not possess design features found in forthcoming Big Three compacts such as a step-down chassis, which allowed a lower body without compromising interior room. The senior Rambler’s body was only three years newer than Studebaker’s so also did not have this feature. However, the Rambler possessed more modern features such as thin-frame doors. Perhaps most importantly, Ramblers had redeeming practical advantages such as unitized construction and a boxy shape that was exceptionally roomy. In contrast, Studebaker suffered from a rattle-prone, body-on-frame design and less rear headroom due to the car’s more teardrop shape.

**Engines —** The Studebaker V8 lacked hydraulic valve lifters and was unduly heavy for a compact; this accentuated the car’s already awkward handling compared to more modern competitors. Meanwhile, Studebaker’s six had an anemic L-head design that, when finally converted to overhead valves in 1961, was still not very competitive in fuel economy, power and reliability.

**Market positioning —**American Motors was well poised to benefit from skyrocketing interest in compacts in the early-60s because it had been a champion of smaller cars for a decade. In contrast, Studebaker spent much of the 1950s vainly trying to reposition its fairly compact cars as direct competitors to the Big Three’s full-size cars by stretching them in ungainly ways (go [here](https://www.indieauto.org/2015/01/20/1951-studebaker-pointing-in-the-wrong-direction/) for further discussion).

[![Image 6: 1958 Studebaker sedan ad](https://i0.wp.com/www.indieauto.org/wp-content/uploads/2015/05/1958-Stude-sedan-col.short_.png?resize=678%2C273&ssl=1)](http://www.oldcarbrochures.org/)

![Image 7: 1958 Studebake wagon front quarter](https://i0.wp.com/www.indieauto.org/wp-content/uploads/2015/05/1958-Studebake-wagon-front-quarter-col.cov_.png?resize=678%2C385&ssl=1)

_The 1958 Studebaker emphasized big luxury in a year when the public began turning to compacts and imports in significant numbers. Note how the illustration (top image) exaggerates the car’s size ([Old Car Brochures](http://www.oldcarbrochures.org/))._

Despite these challenges, newly installed CEO Harold Churchill was determined to move Studebaker-Packard Corporation in a different direction than his predecessor. James Nance had brought the automaker to the brink of insolvency by recklessly trying to offer a full line of cars that competed directly against General Motors, Ford and Chrysler. In contrast, Churchill’s goal was to move “away from head on competition with the Big Three” (Critchlow, [1996](https://www.indieauto.org/2013/04/16/studebaker-the-life-and-death-of-an-american-corporation/); p. 168).

> **_Also see [‘1958 Studebaker: Honesty is the best policy’](https://www.indieauto.org/2020/09/25/1958-studebaker-honesty-is-the-best-policy/)_**

Churchill had the right idea but unwittingly steered Studebaker toward more — not less — direct competition. A big reason why is that he essentially threw away the good parts of Studebaker’s legacy in his understandable efforts to give the struggling automaker a fresh and compelling new image.

## Studebaker designers take out their meat axes

A proposal to develop a compact was among a number of options presented to Studebaker-Packard’s board of directors in late-October of 1957. Other options included 1) restyling the existing line of larger models and 2) offering a compact in addition to current offerings.

The board went with the compact-focused proposal; the larger Studebakers and Packards would be discontinued but the Hawk sporty coupe would be kept in production without major changes.Development of the compact was projected to cost $5.8 million, which was somewhere between the cost of maintaining the existing line — the cheapest option — and offering both compact and larger cars (Ebert, [2013](https://www.indieauto.org/2013/10/26/champion-of-the-lark-harold-churchill-and-the-presidency-of-studebaker-packard-1956-1961/)).

[![Image 8: 1959 Studebaker Lark four-door sedan](https://i0.wp.com/www.indieauto.org/wp-content/uploads/2015/05/1959-Studebaker-Lark-four-door-sedan-ad-col.cov_.png?resize=678%2C382&ssl=1)](http://www.oldcaradvertising.com/)

_The 1959 Lark was positioned in size and price between the senior Rambler and American ([Old Car Advertisements](http://www.oldcaradvertising.com/))._

This decision made sense. Maintaining the status quo was not a viable option in light of the terrible sales for the existing models. Offering a mix of compact and larger cars would have had a lower break-even point (115,000 rather than 121,000 per year) because the larger cars would have pumped up profit margins (Ebert, [2013](https://www.indieauto.org/2013/10/26/champion-of-the-lark-harold-churchill-and-the-presidency-of-studebaker-packard-1956-1961/)). However, the board may have been hesitant to seek $1.4 million in additional financing from banks that had expressed skepticism about Studebaker’s continued viability as an automaker.

What is most striking about the 1959 Studebaker is the degree to which it attempted to make a clean break with the automaker’s past. The resulting compact, which was called the Lark, was a good 31.4 inches shorter than the previous year’s top-of-line President sedan. At 175 inches in length, the Lark was shorter than all other early-60s compacts.

![Image 9: 1959-62 comparison of compact dimensions](https://i0.wp.com/www.indieauto.org/wp-content/uploads/2015/05/1959-62-comparison-of-compact-dimensions-col.short_.png?resize=678%2C285&ssl=1)

Even so, the Lark had a fairly long wheelbase. At 108.5-inches, it was a half-inch more than a senior Rambler’s. This was accomplished by taking a meat axe to the Studebaker body’s front and rear overhangs.That gave the Lark considerably more interior room than a Rambler American, whose 100-inch wheelbase severely restricted rear-seat room.

Studebaker designers had reservations about the shortness of the front overhang. Bob Doehler said that it looked “like one of those cross-country trucks, with no meat ahead of the wheels. The Lark was skimpy in that respect” (Langworth, [1993](https://www.indieauto.org/2013/04/13/studebaker-1946-1966-the-classic-postwar-years/); p. 104).

> **_Also see [‘1959 Studebaker: Was it really design theft?’](https://www.indieauto.org/2014/12/10/1959-studebaker-was-it-really-design-theft/)_**

“Skimpy” is an understatement.I’m hard-pressed to a remember another post-war American passenger-car with such a radically short front end. All of the Big Three trucks in the late-50s and early-60s had longer snouts, although Kaiser-Jeep’s Wagoneer-based truck was similarly shaped.

The downside to the Lark’s truncated look is that it didn’t wear well once the Big Three’s compacts arrived. Even the restyled 1961 American had a front end that looked less dated than the Lark’s despite being based upon an older platform.

![Image 10: 1963 Rambler American](https://i0.wp.com/www.indieauto.org/wp-content/uploads/2016/04/1963-Rambler-American-col.tall_.png?resize=678%2C429&ssl=1)

![Image 11: 1960 Studebaker wagon front](https://i0.wp.com/www.indieauto.org/wp-content/uploads/2015/05/1960-Studebaker-wagon-front-col.tall_.png?resize=678%2C439&ssl=1)

_The 1961-63 Rambler American’s front end had a more modern, horizontal look than the Lark. Pictured is a 1963 American two-door hardtop (top image) and a 1960 Lark wagon._

What about the Plymouth Valiant, which also had a fairly tall radiator grille? The Valiant’s front looks much more contemporary than the Lark’s. This is partly because the Valiant’s cowl is lower and the front overhang is considerably longer. However, the Valiant was also given a Europeanesque bumper that was thin, wide and placed relatively high on the body. The look was sporty rather than agricultural.

[![Image 12: 1960 Plymouth Valiant](https://i0.wp.com/www.indieauto.org/wp-content/uploads/2015/05/1960-Valiant-col.short_.png?resize=678%2C267&ssl=1)](http://www.oldcarbrochures.org/)

_The Valiant had the oddest styling of the Big Three compacts, but its radiator grille looked much sleeker than the Lark’s ([Old Car Brochures](http://www.oldcarbrochures.org/))._

Although the Lark’s front end had a vague family resemblance to the Hawk’s, the casual observer might have mistaken the car as a Rambler rather than a Studebaker. That’s because the Lark’s overall look was so much smaller and less pretentious than its predecessors. Gone were the tacked-on fins, multi-tone trim and chrome-laden grilles.

![Image 13: 1959 and 1955 Studebaker rear ](https://i0.wp.com/www.indieauto.org/wp-content/uploads/2015/05/1959-and-1955-Studebaker-rear-col.cov_.jpg?resize=678%2C382&ssl=1)

_This 1960 Lark is the antithesis of the low-slung and tri-colored 1955 President Speedster in the background — tall, stubby and plain. Note that the hardtop used the same roofline as the sedans._

Also gone was a large trunk. When the Studebaker sedans were last given a major restyling in 1956, trunk space reportedly increased by more than 30 percent. This was accomplished by lengthening the rear overhang four inches and squaring off the fenders’ teardrop shape.

[![Image 14](https://i0.wp.com/www.indieauto.org/wp-content/uploads/2015/05/1959-Stude-trunk-small.png?resize=291%2C218&ssl=1)](http://www.oldcarbrochures.org/)

_Such a high trunk lid was unheard of in that era ([Old Car Brochures](http://www.oldcarbrochures.org/))._

The Lark kept the squared-off fenders but pruned rear overhang more than nine inches. In addition, the trunk lid no longer extended to the bumper. This made the Lark less practical as a family car.

The wagon did not see a reduction in cargo space behind the rear wheels because the basic shape of the D-pillar wasn’t changed (although a number of inches were taken out of the wheelbase in the passenger compartment, thereby requiring redesigned rear-seat doors). Nevertheless, as the photos below show, the Lark looked strikingly different from the 1958 models.

> _**Also see [‘Studebaker Lark V8 is a ‘little mountain goat’’](https://www.indieauto.org/2021/08/05/studebaker-lark-v8-is-a-little-mountain-goat/)**_

Instead of trying to make the rear end look artificially longer, Studebaker designers worked with the natural contour of the wagon’s greenhouse. The result was not particularly modern looking but it was clean and honest . . . almost like a truck-based wagon.

![Image 15: 1960 Studebaker wagon](https://i0.wp.com/www.indieauto.org/wp-content/uploads/2015/05/1960-Studebaker-wagon-rear-col.tall_.png?resize=678%2C419&ssl=1)

![Image 16: 1958 Studebaker wagon ](https://i0.wp.com/www.indieauto.org/wp-content/uploads/2015/05/1958-Studebaker-wagon-rear-col.tall_.png?resize=678%2C448&ssl=1)

_Rarely, if ever, has a wagon’s reskinning resulted in such a dramatically different look. Pictured is a 1960 Lark (top image) and a 1958 Commander Provincial wagon._

## Why weren’t all Larks the same size as the wagon?

The wagon was 9.5 inches longer than the Lark sedans. That’s because it had a 4.5-inch longer wheelbase and its rear overhang wasn’t chopped beyond the original design for that body style, which was introduced in 1954. In retrospect, it’s surprising that Studebaker didn’t give its entire family car line the wagon’s larger footprint.

Nothing was gained by making the Lark so short. Even after Studebaker designers were done with their meat axes, the Lark was still roughly 300 pounds heavier than the Falcon and Corvair. That was too much to be truly competitive when it came to fuel economy, particularly with Studebaker’s ancient L-head six. Meanwhile, the Lark had been pruned too much to be as roomy as larger compacts such as the senior Rambler.

Studebaker eventually realized this. For 1962 the Lark was given a bigger trunk and four-door sedans were moved to the wagon’s 113-inch wheelbase. Entry-level models continued to compete price-wise at the bottom of the compact market, but Studebaker added high-end models.

![Image 17: 1960-62 compact list prices](https://i0.wp.com/www.indieauto.org/wp-content/uploads/2015/05/1960-62-compact-list-prices-col.short_.png?resize=677%2C325&ssl=1)

As you can see from the above graph, Studebaker moved upmarket along with many of its competitors. In doing so, the automaker was returning to the family compact market pioneered by the 1939-52 Champion — which had been the source of Studebaker’s greatest success.

## Studebaker marketing takes a different approach

For 1959 Studebaker could have maintained continuity by calling its new compact the Champion. Instead, marketeers went with the Lark because it would be a companion to the existing Hawk name (Langworth, [1993](https://www.indieauto.org/2013/04/13/studebaker-1946-1966-the-classic-postwar-years/)). Studebaker also ditched its ad agency, Burke, Dowling, Adams, Inc. in favor of D’Arcy Advertising(Ebert, [2013](https://www.indieauto.org/2013/10/26/champion-of-the-lark-harold-churchill-and-the-presidency-of-studebaker-packard-1956-1961/)).

The new agency developed ads that were dramatically different.The most obvious change was how they looked — the terribly stodgy design used in 1958 was replaced with one that was more youthful.Interestingly, ad typography de-emphasized the Studebaker brand in favor of the Lark nameplate. This suggests that management thought the brand was tarnished.

[![Image 18: 1959 Studebaker Lark ad emphasized practicality](https://i0.wp.com/www.indieauto.org/wp-content/uploads/2015/05/1959-Stude-Lark-ad-med.png?resize=505%2C728&ssl=1)](http://www.oldcaradvertising.com/)

_[Old Car Advertisements](http://www.oldcaradvertising.com/)_

Advertisements also tried to turn the Lark’s tall body into a selling point.

For example, the ad to the right does a nice job of presenting the unusually upright fascia as a virtue rather than as ugly. Indeed, that old-fashioned radiator grille epitomized how the Lark was a practical and honest car.

This was a potent message because of public dissatisfaction with late-50s Detroit iron, which had reached a peak of sci-fi stylistic exuberance and quality lapses. The simplicity and directness of this ad anticipated the classic Volkswagen campaigns of the 1960s. Unfortunately, Studebaker did not stick with this approach when it most needed it — after the much swoopier Big Three compacts appeared.

> _**Also see [‘VW’s remarkable defense against Detroit’](https://www.indieauto.org/2014/08/15/vws-remarkable-defense-against-detroit/)**_

By 1962 advertising had slipped back into the old pattern of mimicking Big Three ad-speak. Larks were touted as “America’s new action car” and a “thrilling new definition of glamorous excitement on wheels!”Functional qualities that made Studebaker unique were either de-emphasized or ignored, such as a tall body and no step down that made entry and exit less contorting.

[![Image 19: 1962 Studebaker Lark ad exaggerated car's lowness](https://i0.wp.com/www.indieauto.org/wp-content/uploads/2015/05/1962-Daytona-2-col.short_.png?resize=678%2C350&ssl=1)](http://www.oldcarbrochures.org/)

_Studebaker advertising in 1962 pretended that the Daytona was not tall and stubby ([Old Car Brochures](http://www.oldcarbrochures.org/))._

Perhaps the most incongruous advertising involved the new-for-1962 Daytona line. An emphasis was placed on itemizing fairly generic sporty features while doing little to justify buying a Studebaker rather than a more modern and conventionally stylish car. In addition, Studebaker returned to its mid-50s practice of using illustrations to make its cars look [lower, longer and wider](https://www.indieauto.org/2018/03/12/lower-longer-wider/) than they actually were.

## Sales start strong but then take a nosedive

Management’s decision to take a sharp turn downmarket worked quite well in 1959, before the Big Three entered the compact field. Studebaker’s family car sales almost tripled from 1958, with six-cylinder volume reaching just under 100,000 units.

Alas, it was mostly downhill from there. In 1960 sales fell by a relatively modest 6 percent. More significant was that V8s jumped from a quarter of Lark production to 47 percent. This may reflect that the Big Three did not start to offer V8 compacts until the following year — whereupon Lark V8 production dropped by 55 percent.

![Image 20: 1958-62 output of Studebaker vs VW and American](https://i0.wp.com/www.indieauto.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/09/1958-62-output-of-Studebaker-vs-VW-and-American-col.tall_.png?resize=678%2C445&ssl=1)

Studebaker may have also modestly benefitted in 1960 by offering a two-door hardtop and convertible. Production for both almost reached 16,000, but then plummeted 65 percent in 1961. Direct competition was not the culprit because these two body styles were not widely available in the compact field until 1963. Then what was the problem?

Overall Lark sales were down 45 percent in 1961, but six-cylinder and low-end models saw smaller declines. That suggests Studebaker may have faced its greatest competition from newly introduced premium-priced compacts such as the Pontiac Tempest, Oldsmobile F-85, Buick Special and Mercury Comet.

![Image 21: 1960 Studebaker Lark](https://i0.wp.com/www.indieauto.org/wp-content/uploads/2015/05/1960-Studebaker-Lark-convertible-front-col.short_.png?resize=678%2C370&ssl=1)

![Image 22: 1960 Studebaker Lark convertible](https://i0.wp.com/www.indieauto.org/wp-content/uploads/2015/05/1960-Studebaker-Lark-convertible-rear-col.short_.png?resize=678%2C366&ssl=1)

_For 1960 Studebaker added a convertible — the brand’s first since 1952. This typically low-volume body style actually outsold the two-door hardtop by almost 400 units in its first year of production._

## How much did dealers contribute to falling sales?

Part of the problem was Studebaker’s increasingly weak dealer network. Thomas E. Bonsall ([2000](https://www.indieauto.org/2013/04/20/more-than-they-promised-the-studebaker-story/)) noted that many of the automaker’s dealers also had franchises with Big Three brands. Between 1960 and 1961, GM, Ford and Chrysler introduced eight compact entries — one for every dealer network serving a popularly priced brand. Not so coincidentally, during that time period 356 “dual” dealers cancelled their Studebaker franchises. There went 14 percent of the automaker’s dealers — “and many of the best,” according to Bonsall ([2000](https://www.indieauto.org/2013/04/20/more-than-they-promised-the-studebaker-story/), p. 342).

> _**Also see [‘Classic film shows human side of Studebaker’s end’](https://www.indieauto.org/2021/01/29/classic-film-shows-human-side-of-studebakers-end/)**_

Patrick R. Foster pointed to “charges that certain Big Three divisions were actively luring old-line Studebaker dealers to drop their Studebaker-Packard franchises and take on theirs” ([2008](https://www.indieauto.org/2013/04/28/studebaker-the-complete-history/), p. 125). But Richard M. Langworth suggested that “dealer raids” were “all very natural in the dog-eat-cat world that is the auto business” ([1993](https://www.indieauto.org/2013/04/13/studebaker-1946-1966-the-classic-postwar-years/), p. 164).

[![Image 23: 1961 Studebaker Lark two-door hardtop](https://i0.wp.com/www.indieauto.org/wp-content/uploads/2015/05/1961-Lark-hrdtp-col.short_.png?resize=678%2C338&ssl=1)](http://www.oldcarbrochures.org/)

_By 1961 even the most stylish Lark, the two-door hardtop, looked downright frumpy compared to the more modern Big Three competition ([Old Car Brochures](http://www.oldcarbrochures.org/))._

To add an additional layer of mystery, in 1967 the _Wall Street Journal_ reported on a draft antitrust complaint written by the Justice Department — but never filed with the courts — that accused GM of violating U.S. antitrust laws. Among the allegations: GM’s dealership strategy was anti-competitive because it had forbidden its dealers from selling anything but GM cars. This practice apparently began around 1919 (Sherefkin, [2008](https://www.autonews.com/article/20080914/OEM02/309149885/stunning-postwar-growth-brought-antitrust-scrutiny-in-the-1950s)). If this is accurate, Studebaker would not have had any dealers dualed with a GM brand. It is also hard to visualize GM trying to raid Studebaker’s dealers given their relative weakness compared to those of larger automakers.

At any rate, the loss of dealers to the Big Three was not the inevitable plight of an independent automaker. For 1961, Rambler production was down by 18 percent in this recessionary year but still managed to become the third best-selling brand. American Motors’ achievement was all the more remarkable because its narrow product line was based upon platforms that were roughly as old as Studebaker’s.

[![Image 24: 1960 Rambler American](https://i0.wp.com/www.indieauto.org/wp-content/uploads/2015/05/1960-American-col.short_.png?resize=678%2C306&ssl=1)](http://www.oldcarbrochures.org/)

_The Rambler American almost outsold the Lark in 1960 despite ancient styling. After a reskinning for 1961, the American trounced the Lark by more than a two-to-one margin ([Old Car Brochures](http://www.oldcarbrochures.org/))._

So why was Rambler flying so high while Studebaker was sliding toward death? At the outset of this post we introduced three big — and perhaps insurmountable — challenges that the South Bend-based automaker faced in its 1959 redesign. Studebaker was mostly unable to work around them. Let’s discuss a few key decisions that, if nothing else, might have pushed death further into the future.

## Myopic zigs and zags proved costly

Studebaker made a number of fatal errors with its 1959 redesign. The automaker vainly tried to use the family car platform in ways that did not maximize its strengths and minimize its weaknesses. This primarily occurred because management focused too much on landing short-term sales.

Coming out with a compact roughly the size of the Lark represented the trendy thing to do in 1959-60. That’s the direction the Big Three went with its first wave of compacts. However, in the long run this was a dead end for Studebaker, both because its basic body was too heavy and tall, and its engines could not deliver competitive gas mileage.

> _**Also see [‘1964 Studebaker: Brooks Stevens hammered final nail in the coffin’](https://www.indieauto.org/2021/04/16/1964-studebaker-brooks-stevens-hammered-final-nail-in-the-coffin/)**_

Although Studebaker eventually realized this, by the time the Lark was moved upmarket it was a case of too little, too late. The 1959 Studebaker should have been sized similarly to the 1962 sedan and wagon, with a wheelbase of 113 inches and a length of around 188 inches. Although entry-level models could have been priced within the ballpark of the Rambler American, Studebaker’s primary competitors would have been the senior Rambler, Mercury Comet and post-1962 Dodge Dart. This market positioning would have required a larger and more accessible trunk than even the 1962 Lark’s.

[![Image 25: 1962 Studebaker Lark had roomier back seat](https://i0.wp.com/www.indieauto.org/wp-content/uploads/2015/05/1962-sedan-col.short_.png?resize=678%2C299&ssl=1)](http://www.oldcarbrochures.org/)

_The 1962 sedans were given a longer wheelbase, which revived a longstanding Studebaker strength — exceptionally good rear-seat legroom ([Old Car Brochures](http://www.oldcarbrochures.org/))._

Minimizing front overhang was a laudable goal in light of Studebaker’s nose-heavy V8 engines. However, designers should have focused more on coming up with sheetmetal that would still be competitive at least three years out. That required a much more horizontal look. This was achievable with high-mounted bumpers and a downward curve to the front fenders and hood.

The same principles that governed front-end styling should have applied to the rear. High-mounted bumpers and more horizontal sculpting would have had more staying power than the Lark’s tall and concave shape.

[![Image 26: 1962 Rambler Ambassador](https://i0.wp.com/www.indieauto.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/07/1962-Rambler-Ambassador-col.short_.png?resize=678%2C329&ssl=1)](http://www.oldcarbrochures.org/)

_The senior Rambler’s platform was only three years newer than Studebaker’s but was kept more current. For example, in 1962 the rear end was redesigned with a more horizontal look and a high-mounted bumper ([Old Car Brochures](http://www.oldcarbrochures.org/))._

A two-door hardtop and convertible were not terribly viable body styles for the Lark once the Big Three came out with much lower and more modern-looking models. Thus, development dollars might have been better spent elsewhere, such as more quickly switching to thin-frame doors (which did not occur until 1963).

But since Studebaker had already introduced a two-door hardtop in 1958, designers might have been able to adapt the nicely shaped roofline to the 113-inch wheelbase. Presumably that would have been impossible on the Lark’s 108.5-inch wheelbase.

[![Image 27: 1958 Studebaker two-door hardtop](https://i0.wp.com/www.indieauto.org/wp-content/uploads/2015/05/1958-Stude-hrdtp-col.short_.png?resize=678%2C249&ssl=1)](http://www.oldcarbrochures.org/)

_In light of Studebaker’s meager resources, it was unfortunate that the two-door hardtop’s unique roofline was used for only one year. Note the high-mounted front bumper ([Old Car Brochures](http://www.oldcarbrochures.org/))._

The photoshopped 1960 Lark hardtop (see below) illustrates some — but not all — of these ideas. A more horizontal look is given to the front and rear but the 108.5-inch wheelbase and swept-back roofline from the sedans were kept. A key takeaway is that the short overhangs did not necessitate an excessively upright, agricultural appearance.

[![Image 28: Real and fake 1960 Studebaker Lark two-door hardtop](https://i0.wp.com/www.indieauto.org/wp-content/uploads/2015/05/1959-Lark-real-and-fake-col.tall_.png?resize=678%2C702&ssl=1)](https://www.flickr.com/photos/olyearth/41794154184/in/album-72157691303804680/)

_Click on image to enlarge; base photo courtesy [Old Car Brochures](http://www.oldcarbrochures.org/)._

The direction sketched here is evolutionary enough that it could have included keeping the Champion nameplate. That might have achieved two useful goals: rehabilitating Studebaker’s all-time-biggest-selling nameplate and emphasizing that the automaker created the first family compact in 1939.

An even more important goal was to avoid having to make costly shifts in the positioning of Studebaker’s family cars. The automaker was simply too small and financially fragile to zig-zag around like it did between 1958 and 1962, when Studebakers were positioned first as full-sized, then as entry-level compacts and then as as family-sized compacts. Compare that to Rambler and VW, both of which had strikingly consistent positioning during this period.

> _**Also see [‘Could Studebaker have come out of the 1970s as successful as Jeep?’](https://www.indieauto.org/2021/04/23/could-studebaker-have-been-as-successful-as-jeep/)**_

It’s true that the deficiencies in Studebaker’s platform and engines would have kept it at a disadvantage to the senior Ramblers. Even so, a larger family compact could have been more competitive — and profitable — than an entry-level compact in 1960-61. If automotive operations had stayed in the black both of those years, the banks might have looked more favorably on financing a more substantial redesign.

Ironically, Churchill — the definitive Studebaker company man — helped kill the automaker by walking away from its legacy.

The interiors were smart, even if the floorboard were not step-down from the door-sills, especially the upper-series Hawks, Daytonas and Avantis. (My next-door neighbor had a new 1963 Avanti, which he loved more than his family, frankly. I rode in it a couple of times. To my 13-year-old senses, it seemed like a driver’s car !) Maybe if Studebaker in 1962 had designed a car as brilliant as the 1963 Rambler Classic, and if it had been engineered with a modern architecture and lower cowl, and styled like the Brook Stevens’ designs, Studebaker might have clung to survival. But alas, even Romney’s Rambler did not survive stupid executive and management decisions. Studebaker, after 1958 and James Nance, never had a chance. Reply

I would agree with you that designers like what they like. The problem is that car design can have commercial consequences. Short-sighted decisions can undercut the viability of an automaker.
